chapter: Chapter 1: Greetings & Introductions — 是 Sentences, Names (姓/叫), 很 + Adjectives
title: Personal Pronouns and 是 (shì) Sentences
theory: Mandarin pronouns don't change form for subject vs. object the way English "I/me" or "he/him" do, and verbs never conjugate for person or number. The core set is 我 (wǒ, I/me), 你 (nǐ, you), 您 (nín, you — polite/formal), 他 (tā, he/him), 她 (tā, she/her), and 它 (tā, it). Note that 他, 她, and 它 are all pronounced identically — the distinction only exists in writing. Plurals are formed by simply adding 们 (men): 我们 (wǒmen, we), 你们 (nǐmen, you all), 他们 (tāmen, they).

是 (shì) is a linking verb that equates a subject with a noun, similar to "am/is/are" in English — but unlike English, it never changes form no matter the subject: 我是, 你是, 他是, 我们是 all use the same 是. The basic pattern is Subject + 是 + Noun: 我是学生 (Wǒ shì xuéshēng) literally "I am student," meaning "I am a student." Chinese has no articles ("a," "an," "the"), so none appear in the sentence.

To negate, place 不 (bù, not) directly before 是: 我不是学生 (Wǒ bú shì xuéshēng), "I am not a student." (Note the tone change: 不 is normally fourth tone, but shifts to second tone — bú — before another fourth-tone syllable like 是; this is written in pinyin but not in hanzi.) A simple yes/no question can be formed by adding the particle 吗 (ma) to the end of a statement — covered in full in Chapter 2.
pattern: S + 是 + N　·　S + 不是 + N

chapter: Chapter 1: Greetings & Introductions — 是 Sentences, Names (姓/叫), 很 + Adjectives
title: Asking and Giving Names — 姓 (xìng) and 叫 (jiào)
theory: Chinese has two distinct verbs for names, and they are not interchangeable. 姓 (xìng) is used specifically for surnames/family names: 我姓王 (Wǒ xìng Wáng), "My surname is Wang." 叫 (jiào) is used for a full name or given name: 我叫王明 (Wǒ jiào Wáng Míng), "My name is Wang Ming" (also usable with just a given name in casual contexts).

Asking someone's surname politely uses the fixed formula 您贵姓？ (Nín guì xìng?, literally "your honorable surname?") — 贵 here doesn't function as an ordinary adjective and 贵姓 shouldn't be broken apart or reused elsewhere. A neutral, everyday way to ask is simply 你姓什么？ (Nǐ xìng shénme?).

Asking for a full name uses 你叫什么名字？ (Nǐ jiào shénme míngzi?, "What is your name?") — literally "you are-called what name." 什么 (shénme, "what") sits directly in the object slot of the sentence rather than moving to the front the way English "what" does; this word-order rule — a question word stays exactly where the answer would go — applies to every Chinese question word and is covered fully in Chapter 3.
名字 (míngzi) means "name" as a noun and can also be used with 是: 你的名字是什么？ is grammatical, though 你叫什么名字？ is far more common in everyday speech.
pattern: S + 姓 + Surname。　·　S + 叫 + Full/Given Name。

chapter: Chapter 1: Greetings & Introductions — 是 Sentences, Names (姓/叫), 很 + Adjectives
title: Adjectival Predicates with 很 (hěn)
theory: This is one of the first true traps for English speakers: Chinese adjectives act as verbs on their own and do NOT need 是 to link them to the subject. You cannot say 我是累 to mean "I am tired" — that is simply ungrammatical. Instead, the adjective directly follows the subject: 我累 (Wǒ lèi).

In practice, however, a bare adjective standing completely alone as the predicate (我累。) can sound clipped or implicitly contrastive — as if you mean "I'm tired (unlike someone else)." To avoid that unwanted implication in a plain, neutral statement, Chinese speakers insert 很 (hěn, "very") before the adjective: 我很累 (Wǒ hěn lèi). In this everyday use, 很 is largely grammatical glue rather than true emphasis — it does not usually translate as "very" unless it is spoken with stress. This pattern, S + 很 + Adj, is the default, neutral way to say "[Subject] is [adjective]."

Negation drops 很 entirely and uses 不 (bù) directly before the adjective: 我不忙 (Wǒ bù máng), "I'm not busy." Adding 很 back into a negative sentence (不很...) is possible but shifts the meaning toward "not very..." rather than a flat negation.
Because the adjective already functions as the predicate, never insert 是 into this pattern — 是 is reserved for linking two nouns (Chapter 1, Section 1), not a subject to an adjective.
pattern: S + 很 + Adj.　·　S + 不 + Adj.

chapter: Chapter 2: Questions and Possession — 吗 and 的
title: Yes/No Questions with 吗 (ma)
theory: The simplest way to turn any statement into a yes/no question in Mandarin is to add the particle 吗 (ma) to the very end — no change to word order, and no auxiliary "do/does/is" the way English requires. 你忙 (Nǐ máng, "You are busy") becomes 你忙吗？ (Nǐ máng ma?, "Are you busy?") simply by appending 吗.

This works with any statement type already covered: 你是学生吗？(Nǐ shì xuéshēng ma?, "Are you a student?") and 他很高吗？(Tā hěn gāo ma?, "Is he tall?") both follow the same rule — state the sentence, then add 吗.

One important restriction: 吗 can only be added to a sentence that has no other question word already in it. A sentence using 什么 (shénme, what), 谁 (shéi, who), or similar words is already a question and cannot also take 吗 — mixing the two is a common beginner error covered in full in Chapter 3, on question words.

Mandarin has no single word for a bare "yes" or "no." To answer a 吗 question, you affirm or deny by repeating the key verb from the question: 是 or 不是 for a 是-question, 忙 or 不忙 for an adjective question. 是的 (shì de) is also commonly used as a general-purpose "yes."

examples.hanzi: A: 你是学生吗？B: 是，我是学生。
examples.pinyin: A: Nǐ shì xuéshēng ma? B: Shì, wǒ shì xuéshēng.
examples.english: A: Are you a student? B: Yes, I am a student.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì nǐ de shū ma?

chapter: Chapter 2: Questions and Possession — 吗 and 的
title: The Possessive Particle 的 (de)
theory: 的 (de, neutral tone) marks possession, roughly matching English "'s" or "of." The pattern is Possessor + 的 + Noun, in the opposite order from "of" but the same order as "'s": 我的书 (wǒ de shū) is literally "I's book," meaning "my book." 老师的手机 (lǎoshī de shǒujī) is "the teacher's phone."

的 is frequently dropped for close, personal relationships — especially family members and, often, close friends — when the meaning is unambiguous without it: 我妈妈 (wǒ māma, "my mom") and 我朋友 (wǒ péngyou, "my friend") both sound natural without 的, whereas dropping it from 我的书 would sound off. There's no hard rule for exactly where the line falls; it's learned by exposure, but the general pattern is: the closer/more personal the relationship, the more natural it is to omit 的.

的 does more than mark possession — the same particle attaches almost any descriptive word or phrase to a following noun (e.g. "red 的 apple", "the book that I bought 的"), a broader pattern covered in a later chapter. For now, it's enough to recognize 的 as "the noun that follows belongs to, or is linked to, whatever came before 的."

A pronunciation note for later reading: 得 and 地 are both also pronounced "de" in their unstressed grammatical uses, but they mark completely different constructions (verb complements and adverbial phrases, respectively) and are not interchangeable with 的 in writing, even though they can sound identical in casual speech.

examples.english: She is my friend. (的 dropped — close relationship)

chapter: Chapter 3: Question Words — 什么, 谁, 哪, 怎么样
title: 什么 (what) and 谁 (who)
theory: Chinese question words don't move to the front of the sentence the way English "what/who" do. Instead, they sit exactly in the slot where the answer would go — this is sometimes called "question word in situ." 你喝什么？ (Nǐ hē shénme?, "What are you drinking?") mirrors the structure of its answer, 我喝茶 ("I drink tea"), with 什么 simply replacing 茶.

什么 (shénme, "what") attaches directly before a noun to ask "what/which kind of" that noun — 什么书 (shénme shū, "what book") — or stands alone as the object of a verb: 你要什么？ (Nǐ yào shénme?, "What do you want?").

谁 (shéi, also read shuí in careful/formal speech) means "who," and like 什么, stays in its normal sentence position: 他是谁？ (Tā shì shéi?, "Who is he?") mirrors 他是老师 with 谁 replacing 老师. As a subject, it simply starts the sentence because that's where the subject naturally goes, not because it's a question word: 谁是老师？ (Shéi shì lǎoshī?, "Who is the teacher?").
Because these are already full questions, none of them ever combine with 吗 — the rule first introduced in Chapter 2 and true for every question word in this chapter.
pattern: S + V + 什么？　·　谁 + V...？ / S + 是 + 谁？

chapter: Chapter 3: Question Words — 什么, 谁, 哪, 怎么样
title: 哪 (which) and Asking Nationality — 哪国人
theory: 哪 (nǎ, "which") always attaches to a measure word or noun — it can't stand completely alone the way 什么 sometimes can: 哪个 (nǎge, "which one," using the general measure word 个), 哪本书 (nǎ běn shū, "which book").
哪儿 (nǎr) / 哪里 (nǎli) both mean "where," and are used together with 在 to ask about location: 你在哪儿？ (Nǐ zài nǎr?, "Where are you?").

A very common fixed pattern for asking someone's nationality combines 哪 with 国 (guó, "country"): 你是哪国人？ (Nǐ shì nǎ guó rén?, literally "you are which-country person," meaning "What's your nationality?"). The answer swaps in a country name the same way: 我是美国人 (Wǒ shì Měiguó rén, "I am American"), following the general [Country] + 人 pattern used for nationalities.
Same in-situ rule as always: 哪 and its phrases sit exactly where the answer word would go, and never combine with 吗.
pattern: 哪 + M/N...？　·　S + 是 + 哪国人？

chapter: Chapter 3: Question Words — 什么, 谁, 哪, 怎么样
title: 怎么样 (how about / how is it) for Opinions and Suggestions
theory: 怎么样 (zěnmeyàng) asks for an opinion or evaluation of something already mentioned, roughly "how is it?" or "how about...?": 这个怎么样？ (Zhège zěnmeyàng?, "How's this one? / What do you think of this?"). It typically comes at the very end of the sentence.

A very common everyday use is proposing plans — placing 怎么样 after a suggestion softens it into an invitation rather than a command: 我们去看电影，怎么样？ (Wǒmen qù kàn diànyǐng, zěnmeyàng?, "Let's go watch a movie — how about it?").

Don't confuse 怎么样 with 怎么 (zěnme) alone, which asks "how" in the sense of manner or method — how something is done — not an opinion: 这个字怎么写？ (Zhège zì zěnme xiě?, "How do you write this character?"). 怎么样 always asks for an evaluation or reaction; 怎么 always asks for a method.

examples.english: Let's go get coffee — how about it?
How do you write this character?

chapter: Chapter 4: Follow-Ups and Adverbs — 呢, 也, 都, 一起
title: The Follow-Up Question Particle 呢 (ne)
theory: 呢 (ne) lets you ask "what about ___?" without repeating the whole question, by attaching it directly to a noun or pronoun: 我很好，你呢？ (Wǒ hěn hǎo, nǐ ne?), "I'm good, and you?" It picks up whatever was just asked or stated and redirects it at a new subject.

呢 can also attach to a noun phrase on its own, without an explicit preceding question, when the context makes clear that something is being sought or is unaccounted for — this typically translates as "where is...?": 我的手机呢？(Wǒ de shǒujī ne?), "Where's my phone?"

Distinguish 呢 from 吗 (Chapter 2): 呢 does not turn an arbitrary statement into a yes/no question by itself — it needs either a preceding question to reference, or a clear "where is X" context. It is never added just to mean a neutral tag question like English "..., right?"

examples.hanzi: A: 你好吗？B: 我很好，谢谢，你呢？
examples.pinyin: A: Nǐ hǎo ma? B: Wǒ hěn hǎo, xièxie, nǐ ne?
examples.english: A: How are you? B: I'm well, thanks, and you?

chapter: Chapter 4: Follow-Ups and Adverbs — 呢, 也, 都, 一起
title: 也 (also) and 都 (all/both) — Placement Before the Verb
theory: 也 (yě, "also/too") and 都 (dōu, "all/both") are adverbs that must sit directly before the verb (or before 是 / 很+adjective) — never at the end of the sentence the way English "too" or "also" usually lands: 我也是学生 (Wǒ yě shì xuéshēng), "I am also a student," not 我是学生也.
都 sums up a plural or multi-part subject that comes before it: 我们都是学生 (Wǒmen dōu shì xuéshēng), "We are all students." It cannot be used with a clearly singular subject to mean "very/completely."
When both appear together, the fixed order is 也都 (yě dōu), never 都也: 他们也都很忙 (Tāmen yě dōu hěn máng), "They are also all busy."

Negating a 都 sentence is a classic source of ambiguity: 我们都不是学生 (dōu before 不) means "none of us are students," while 我们不都是学生 (不 before dōu) means "not all of us are students" (i.e., some are, some aren't). The position of 不 relative to 都 changes what's actually being negated.
pattern: S + 也/都 + V.　·　S + 也都 + V.

examples.pinyin: Tāmen yě dōu shì Zhōngguó rén.

chapter: Chapter 4: Follow-Ups and Adverbs — 呢, 也, 都, 一起
title: 一起 (yìqǐ) — Together
theory: 一起 (yìqǐ, "together") is an adverb, so — like 也 and 都 earlier in this chapter — it must go before the verb, not after, unlike English "together," which usually trails the sentence: 我们一起去 (Wǒmen yìqǐ qù), "Let's go together," not 我们去一起.

一起 very often pairs with 跟 (gēn, "with") or 和 (hé, "and/with") to specify who the action is done together with: 我跟你一起去 (Wǒ gēn nǐ yìqǐ qù), "I'll go together with you." The 跟/和-phrase comes before 一起, both still before the verb.
A common invitation pattern combines 一起 with 吧 (ba, a suggestion particle covered in a later chapter): 我们一起吃饭吧 (Wǒmen yìqǐ chīfàn ba), "Let's eat together."
pattern: S + (跟/和 + N +) 一起 + V。

examples.hanzi: 你想跟我们一起吃饭吗？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng gēn wǒmen yìqǐ chīfàn ma?
examples.english: Do you want to eat with us?

chapter: Chapter 5: Location and Existence — 在, 有, and Location Words
title: 在 (zài) as "To Be Located At"
theory: As a main verb, 在 (zài) means "to be located at" and directly links a subject to a place: 我在家 (Wǒ zài jiā), "I am at home." No 是 is needed or used here — inserting 是 before 在 (我是在家) is a common but incorrect beginner habit.

Place words often need a location word attached to sound natural: 这儿/这里 (here), 那儿/那里 (there), or a suffix like 里 (inside) / 上 (on) attached to a plain noun: 书在桌子上 (Shū zài zhuōzi shang), "The book is on the table." A bare noun like 桌子 alone usually cannot stand in as a location without 上/里/etc. — the full set of these location words is covered later in this chapter.

在 also functions as a preposition marking where an action takes place, positioned before the verb: 我在家吃饭 (Wǒ zài jiā chīfàn), "I eat at home." Note that the location phrase (在 + place) comes before the verb, the reverse of English's "I eat at home," where "at home" trails the verb.
Negation uses 不在: 他不在家 (Tā bú zài jiā), "He is not at home."
pattern: S + 在 + Place.　·　S + 在 + Place + V.

examples.english: The book is on the table.

chapter: Chapter 5: Location and Existence — 在, 有, and Location Words
title: 有 (yǒu) for Possession and Existence
theory: 有 (yǒu, "to have") links a subject to something it possesses: 我有一个手机 (Wǒ yǒu yí ge shǒujī), "I have a phone." Unlike 是 and most other verbs, 有 is never negated with 不 — it uniquely takes 没 instead: 我没有手机 (Wǒ méiyǒu shǒujī), "I don't have a phone" (不有 is simply ungrammatical).

有 also states that something exists at a place, with the place named first: Place + 有 + N, e.g. 桌子上有一本书 (Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū), "There is a book on the table" (literally "table-on has a book"). This is the mirror image of the 在 pattern from the previous section: 在 puts the specific, already-known thing first and the place after (书在桌子上), while 有 puts the place first and the new/unspecified thing after.
A very common yes/no question form with 有 is 有没有 ("have-not-have"), an alternative to adding 吗: 你有没有手机？ means the same as 你有手机吗？ — both are correct and equally natural.
pattern: S + 有/没有 + N.　·　Place + 有 + N.

examples.pinyin: Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū.
examples.english: There's a book on the table.

chapter: Chapter 5: Location and Existence — 在, 有, and Location Words
title: Location Words — 上, 下, 里, 外, 前面, 后面, 旁边
theory: As flagged earlier in this chapter, a plain noun in Chinese usually cannot serve as a location on its own — it needs a location word attached, most often as a suffix directly after the noun. The core set: 上 (shàng, on/above), 下 (xià, under/below), 里 (lǐ, inside), 外 (wài, outside), 前面 (qiánmiàn, in front), 后面 (hòumiàn, behind), and 旁边 (pángbiān, next to/beside). Note 前/后 almost always appear with 面 (miàn) attached in everyday use, while 上/下/里/外 can often stand alone as a single-syllable suffix.

These attach directly to the noun whose position they describe, forming a compound location phrase used exactly like any other place word with 在 or 有: 桌子上 (zhuōzi shang, "on the table"), 学校里 (xuéxiào li, "inside the school"), 书店旁边 (shūdiàn pángbiān, "next to the bookstore").

When the location is a place that's already inherently a "place" (like 学校 school, or 家 home) rather than a plain object, 里 is often optional or dropped in casual speech — 我在学校 is already fine on its own, and 我在学校里 is also correct and slightly more explicit. Object nouns like 桌子 (table) or 书包 (backpack) almost always need the suffix: 书在书包里 (Shū zài shūbāo li), "The book is in the backpack," not 书在书包.
pattern: N + 上/下/里/外/前面/后面/旁边

examples.english: The cat is under the table.
The book is in the backpack.
My home is next to the school.
He is in front of me.

chapter: Chapter 6: Numbers, Measure Words & Measurements — 几/多少, 岁/多大, 多 + Adj, 每
title: Numbers 0–100
theory: Numbers 0–10 are single syllables: 零(0) 一(1) 二(2) 三(3) 四(4) 五(5) 六(6) 七(7) 八(8) 九(9) 十(10). Numbers 11–19 are built as 十 + digit: 十一 (11), 十五 (15). Multiples of ten are digit + 十: 二十 (20), 五十 (50). Numbers in between combine both, largest place value first: 二十三 (23) is literally "two-ten-three."

一百 is 100. Between 100 and 999, a "filler" 零 (líng) is inserted whenever a tens digit is skipped, to signal the gap: 一百零五 (105, "one hundred zero five") vs. 一百五十 (150, no 零 needed since the tens digit is present).

When a number is actually counting a noun (rather than being said in isolation, like reading a phone number), a measure word must sit between the number and the noun — covered in the next section. Also note: when 二 would be the count of objects (not the abstract number "two" on its own, like in "chapter two"), it is normally replaced by 两 (liǎng): 两个人 (liǎng ge rén, "two people"), not 二个人.
pattern: [tens]十[ones]　·　两 (not 二) + Measure Word + N

chapter: Chapter 6: Numbers, Measure Words & Measurements — 几/多少, 岁/多大, 多 + Adj, 每
title: Measure Words with 个, and 几 vs. 多少
theory: Chinese requires a measure word (also called a classifier) between a number and the noun it counts — English does this only occasionally ("two sheets of paper"), but Chinese does it always. 个 (ge) is the default, all-purpose measure word, usable for people, most everyday objects, and abstract nouns when no more specific measure word is known: 一个人 (yí ge rén, "one person"), 三个苹果 (sān ge píngguǒ, "three apples"). Later chapters introduce noun-specific measure words, like 本 for bound books and 件 for garments.

To ask "how many," Chinese uses two different words depending on the expected size of the answer. 几 (jǐ) expects a small number, roughly under ten, and is always followed directly by a measure word: 你有几个朋友？ (Nǐ yǒu jǐ ge péngyou?, "How many friends do you have?"). 多少 (duōshao) is neutral about size and can be followed by a measure word or, very commonly, skip it entirely: 你有多少钱？ (Nǐ yǒu duōshao qián?, "How much money do you have?").

Because 几 implies "a small number," it's the natural choice for counting family members, hours, or a handful of items, while 多少 is the default for money, population, or anything that could plausibly be a large, open-ended number.
pattern: 几 + Measure Word + N...?　·　多少 + (Measure Word) + N...?

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ ge rén?
examples.english: How many people are in your family?
How many students does this school have?

chapter: Chapter 6: Numbers, Measure Words & Measurements — 几/多少, 岁/多大, 多 + Adj, 每
title: Asking and Stating Age — 岁 and 多大
theory: 岁 (suì) is the measure word for years of age, attaching directly after a number: 我十九岁 (Wǒ shíjiǔ suì), "I am 19 years old." No verb "to be" is used at all — 是 does NOT normally appear in a statement of age; inserting it (我是十九岁) is a common but incorrect beginner habit, parallel to the 很+adjective rule in Chapter 1.

To ask a child's or clearly young person's age, 几岁 is standard, following the "small number" logic from the previous section: 你几岁？ (Nǐ jǐ suì?). For an adult, or anyone whose age isn't obviously small, 多大 is used instead: 你多大？ (Nǐ duō dà?, literally "how big are you," meaning "how old are you?").

For an elderly person, a more respectful question is used instead — 您多大年纪？ (Nín duō dà niánjì?) — pairing the polite pronoun 您 from Chapter 1 with 多大. Using 几岁 on a visibly adult stranger can sound like you assume they're a small child, so matching the question to the person's apparent age matters.
pattern: S + Number + 岁。　·　几岁？/ 多大？

examples.english: How old are you? (to a child)
How old are you? (to an adult)
How old are you? (polite, to an elder)

chapter: Chapter 6: Numbers, Measure Words & Measurements — 几/多少, 岁/多大, 多 + Adj, 每
title: Asking Measurements and Duration with 多 (duō)
theory: Beyond age (多大, previous section), 多 (duō) combines with a range of adjectives to ask "how [adjective]" for measurements — the same pattern-shape as 多大, just swapping the adjective: 多高 (duō gāo, "how tall"), 多长 (duō cháng, "how long"), 多重 (duō zhòng, "how heavy"), 多远 (duō yuǎn, "how far").
The answer states the measurement directly with a number and unit, without needing 多 again: 你多高？ (Nǐ duō gāo?, "How tall are you?") → 我一米七 (Wǒ yì mǐ qī, "I'm 1.7 meters").

多长时间 (duō cháng shíjiān, literally "how long [a] time") specifically asks about duration — how long an action or state lasts — distinct from asking about a point in time (几点, next chapter): 你要学多长时间？ (Nǐ yào xué duō cháng shíjiān?, "How long do you want to study for?").

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yào xué duō cháng shíjiān?
examples.english: How long do you want to study for?

chapter: Chapter 6: Numbers, Measure Words & Measurements — 几/多少, 岁/多大, 多 + Adj, 每
title: 每 (měi) + Measure Word — "Every ___"
theory: 每 (měi, "every/each") takes the same measure-word slot as a number: 每 + Measure Word + Noun, exactly mirroring the numbers-and-measure-words pattern from earlier in this chapter. 每天 (měi tiān, "every day") and 每个人 (měi ge rén, "every person/everyone") are the two most common combinations — note 天 (day), like 年 (year), functions as its own measure word and doesn't need 个 inserted.

Sentences with 每 very often pair with 都 (Chapter 4) directly before the verb, to emphasize that the statement holds for every single instance without exception: 我每天都学习汉语 (Wǒ měi tiān dōu xuéxí Hànyǔ), "I study Chinese every day (without exception)." Dropping 都 (我每天学习汉语) is grammatical but slightly less emphatic.

每 differs from a quantity word like 一点儿 in that it doesn't measure how much of something exists — it universally quantifies over a category ("each and every one"), always paired with a countable noun via a measure word, never with a mass/uncountable amount.
pattern: 每 + M + N (+ 都) + V。

examples.pinyin: Wǒ měi tiān dōu xuéxí Hànyǔ.
Měi ge rén dōu xǐhuan tā.
Wǒ měi nián dōu qù Zhōngguó.
examples.english: I go to China every year.

examples.pinyin: Měi ge xuésheng dōu yǒu shǒujī.

chapter: Chapter 7: Time Expressions — 点, Time Word Order, 从...到...
title: Telling Time with 点
theory: 点 (diǎn) marks the hour, directly after the number: 三点 (sān diǎn, "3 o'clock"). Minutes follow the hour: 三点十分 (sān diǎn shí fēn, "3:10" — 分 fēn means minutes, and is often dropped informally: 三点十). For 15 and 45 minutes, 刻 (kè, "quarter") is common: 三点一刻 (3:15), 三点三刻 (3:45), alongside the fully spelled-out 三点十五(分) / 三点四十五(分).
半 (bàn, "half") replaces "thirty minutes" for the half hour: 三点半 (sān diǎn bàn, "3:30") is the natural way to say it, rather than 三点三十分, though the latter is also understood.
Unlike numbers used for plain counting, "two o'clock" uses 两 rather than 二: 两点 (liǎng diǎn), not 二点 — the same 两-vs-二 rule from the numbers section.
Asking the time uses 几, the "small number" question word, since clock hours are always 1–12: 现在几点？ (Xiànzài jǐ diǎn?, "What time is it now?").
pattern: 现在 + Time + 点 (+ 分/刻/半)。

chapter: Chapter 7: Time Expressions — 点, Time Word Order, 从...到...
title: Time Words and Word Order (今天, 明天, 昨天, 星期)
theory: Days of the week use 星期 (xīngqī) + a number: 星期一 (Monday) through 星期六 (Saturday), with Sunday as the one exception, 星期天 or 星期日. 今天 (jīntiān, today), 明天 (míngtiān, tomorrow), and 昨天 (zuótiān, yesterday) are frequent companions.

The single most important rule for all time words — clock times, days, dates, 今天/明天/昨天 — is word order: they go before the verb, typically right after the subject (or, less commonly, at the very start of the sentence), never at the end, unlike English's habit of putting "tomorrow" or "at 3 o'clock" after the verb phrase. 我明天去学校 (Wǒ míngtiān qù xuéxiào), "I'm going to school tomorrow" — not 我去学校明天.

Larger time units precede smaller ones, the reverse of typical American date order: year → month → day → time. E.g. 二零二六年八月十四号下午三点 ("2026, August 14th, 3pm") reads largest-to-smallest all the way through.

examples.english: Which day of the week are you free?

chapter: Chapter 7: Time Expressions — 点, Time Word Order, 从...到...
title: 从...到... (cóng...dào...) — "From...To..."
theory: 从 (cóng, "from") marks a starting point and 到 (dào, "to/until") marks an ending point, together bracketing a range of time or place: 我从九点到十二点上课 (Wǒ cóng jiǔ diǎn dào shí'èr diǎn shàngkè), "I have class from 9 to 12." The whole 从...到... phrase, like every time and place phrase covered so far, goes before the verb.
Either half can be used alone when only one endpoint matters: 从今天开始 (cóng jīntiān kāishǐ, "starting from today") uses only 从; 到星期五 (dào xīngqīwǔ, "until/by Friday") uses only 到.

The same 从...到... frame works for physical distance, not just time, following exactly the same word order: 从我家到学校很近 (Cóng wǒ jiā dào xuéxiào hěn jìn), "It's very close from my house to school" — here the whole 从...到... phrase acts as the subject of the 很近 adjectival-predicate sentence from Chapter 1.
pattern: 从 + Start + 到 + End + V。

examples.hanzi: 我从九点到十二点上课。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ cóng jiǔ diǎn dào shí'èr diǎn shàngkè.
Cóng wǒ jiā dào xuéxiào hěn jìn.
examples.english: It's very close from my house to school.

examples.hanzi: 我们从星期一到星期五都上班。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen cóng xīngqīyī dào xīngqīwǔ dōu shàngbān.
examples.english: We work from Monday to Friday.

examples.hanzi: 从今天开始，我每天都学习。
examples.pinyin: Cóng jīntiān kāishǐ, wǒ měi tiān dōu xuéxí.
examples.english: Starting today, I'll study every day.

chapter: Chapter 8: Going Places and Doing Things — 去/来 + Verb
title: 去/来 + Verb Serialization
theory: To express going somewhere in order to do something, Chinese places two verbs back-to-back with no connecting word: 去 (qù, "go") or 来 (lái, "come") directly followed by the action verb: 我去买东西 (Wǒ qù mǎi dōngxi), literally "I go buy things," meaning "I'm going to buy things / going shopping." English needs "to" or "and" here ("go to buy" / "go and buy"); Chinese needs nothing.

The place, if mentioned, sits between 去/来 and the second verb: 我去商店买东西 (Wǒ qù shāngdiàn mǎi dōngxi), "I'm going to the store to buy things." This mirrors the rule from Chapter 5 that a place phrase comes before the verb it modifies, not after.

来 works the same way but implies motion toward the speaker rather than away: 你来我家吃饭吧 (Nǐ lái wǒ jiā chīfàn ba), "Come to my place to eat" (吧 here is a gentle suggestion particle, covered fully in a later chapter).

This construction is one specific case of a broader pattern called "serial verbs" (stringing multiple verbs in one sentence with no connector) that recurs throughout Chinese; 去/来 + Verb is simply the most common and earliest-learned instance of it.

examples.english: I'm going to the store to buy things.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ lái wǒ jiā chīfàn ba.
examples.english: Come to my place to eat.
He goes to school to study Chinese.

chapter: Chapter 9: Modal Verbs — 想, 要, 会, 能
title: 想 and 要 — Wanting To
theory: Both 想 (xiǎng) and 要 (yào) can precede a verb to mean "want to," but they differ in strength. 想 expresses a wish or inclination — softer, closer to "would like to": 我想去中国 (Wǒ xiǎng qù Zhōngguó), "I'd like to go to China." 要 is more direct and can sound like a firm intention or even a demand, depending on tone: 我要去中国 (Wǒ yào qù Zhōngguó), "I want to / am going to go to China."

要 (but not 想) can also work as a plain transitive verb directly in front of a noun, meaning "want [a thing]": 我要一杯咖啡 (Wǒ yào yì bēi kāfēi), "I want a coffee." 想 needs a verb after it in this pattern — 我想要咖啡 is fine too (combining both softens 要 slightly), but a bare 我想咖啡 sounds incomplete.

Negation differs meaningfully between the two. 不想 simply means "don't want to / don't feel like it": 我不想去 (Wǒ bù xiǎng qù), "I don't feel like going." 不要, however, is much stronger and usually functions as a prohibition or command — "don't!": 不要说话！(Bú yào shuōhuà!, "Don't talk!") — so it isn't just the neutral opposite of wanting something.

examples.english: He doesn't feel like going to school.

chapter: Chapter 9: Modal Verbs — 想, 要, 会, 能
title: 会 and 能 — Ability, Permission, and Prediction
theory: 会 (huì) expresses ability gained through learning or practice — a skill: 我会说中文 (Wǒ huì shuō Zhōngwén), "I can speak Chinese" (I've learned how). It's not used for things anyone can physically do without having learned them.

能 (néng) expresses ability due to physical capability, circumstance, or permission at a given moment, rather than a learned skill. 我能游泳 (Wǒ néng yóuyǒng) can mean "I'm physically able to swim right now (e.g. the pool is open, I'm not injured)," which is distinct from 我会游泳, "I know how to swim" (as a skill). 能 is also the natural choice for asking permission: 我能进来吗？(Wǒ néng jìnlái ma?, "May I come in?").

The two overlap in many everyday sentences, and native speakers sometimes use them interchangeably for skills — but the core distinction (learned skill = 会, situational capability/permission = 能) is the reliable rule to lean on as a learner. Negate both with 不: 不会 ("don't know how"), 不能 ("can't, due to circumstance or not allowed").

会 has a second, seemingly unrelated use worth knowing early: it can also express a prediction or likelihood about the future, closer to English "will" — 明天会下雨 (Míngtiān huì xià yǔ), "It will rain tomorrow." This isn't about anyone's learned skill; it's a forecast or expectation. Context almost always makes clear which sense of 会 is meant, since a sentence about weather or future events obviously isn't about a skill.

examples.english: I can speak a little Chinese.
I don't know how to drive.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ néng wèn yí ge wèntí ma?

chapter: Chapter 10: 了 — Completed Actions and Change of State
title: 了 After the Verb — Marking a Completed Action
theory: Placed directly after a verb, 了 (le) signals that the action was completed — most often used when a specific quantity or detail of the object is mentioned: 我买了一本书 (Wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū), "I bought a book." The 了 attaches to the verb 买, not to the sentence as a whole.

This is not a general past-tense marker the way English "-ed" is — it doesn't just mean "sometime in the past." A generic past action often doesn't need 了 at all, especially when a time word already makes the timing clear, or the sentence describes a habitual or general past state. Adding an unnecessary 了 here is one of the most common overcorrections English speakers make.
Negating a completed action uses 没(有), and 了 is dropped entirely: 我没买书 (Wǒ méi mǎi shū), "I didn't buy a book" — never 我没买了书. This is a hard rule: 了 and 没 never co-occur on the same verb.
pattern: S + V + 了 + (Number + M + N)。　·　S + 没(有) + V + (O)。

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū.
Tā chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
Zuótiān wǒ kàn le yí ge diànyǐng.

chapter: Chapter 10: 了 — Completed Actions and Change of State
title: 了 At the End of a Sentence — Change of State
theory: Placed at the very end of a sentence (after the object, if any, or after an adjective), 了 signals that a new situation has come into being — something is different now compared to before: 我是学生了 (Wǒ shì xuéshēng le), "I'm a student now (I wasn't before)." 冷了 (Lěng le), "It's gotten cold (it wasn't before)."

This use is common with adjectives to describe a change: 他高了 (Tā gāo le), "He's gotten tall(er)," and with 不 + verb/adjective + 了 to announce that something has stopped or is about to stop: 我不去了 (Wǒ bú qù le), "I'm not going (after all) — a change of plan," which is distinct from a plain 我不去, a neutral statement with no implication that plans changed.

The two uses of 了 covered in this chapter — after-verb "completed action" and sentence-final "change of state" — can combine into a single 了 when the completed action is itself the whole point and nothing follows: 我吃了 (Wǒ chī le) standing alone means "I've eaten (as of now)," functioning as both at once. Context and position, not different characters, are what distinguish the two uses — it's the same 了 throughout.

examples.english: It's 8 o'clock now (as of just now).

chapter: Chapter 11: Degree and Politeness — 太...了 and 请
title: 太...了 (tài...le) — "Too ___"
theory: 太...了 wraps around an adjective (or occasionally a verb phrase) to mean "too [adjective]" — an excessive degree, usually with a negative or surprised connotation: 太贵了 (tài guì le), "too expensive." Unlike 很 (Chapter 1), which is a fairly neutral default, 太...了 always signals "more than is desirable or expected."

The 了 here is essentially fixed to this pattern in everyday speech — 太贵 alone, without 了, is understood but sounds noticeably less natural/complete than 太贵了. This 了 is close in spirit to the sentence-final "change of state" 了 from the previous chapter, marking that this degree has now been reached or realized.

太...了 can also express strong positive reactions, not just complaints, depending on tone and context: 太好了！(Tài hǎo le!, "That's great!" — literally "too good") is one of the most common exclamations in everyday Chinese, despite 太 literally meaning "excessively."

chapter: Chapter 11: Degree and Politeness — 太...了 and 请
title: 请 (qǐng) + Verb — Polite Requests
theory: 请 (qǐng) placed directly before a verb turns a sentence into a polite request or invitation, similar to English "please": 请坐 (Qǐng zuò), "Please sit," 请进 (Qǐng jìn), "Please come in."

请 can also be used as a standalone verb meaning "to invite" or "to treat (someone to something)," most commonly in 我请你 (Wǒ qǐng nǐ, "It's my treat / I'm inviting you [to pay for this]"), often heard when offering to pay for a meal: 我请你吃饭 (Wǒ qǐng nǐ chīfàn), "Let me treat you to a meal."

请问 (Qǐng wèn, literally "please ask," meaning "excuse me, may I ask...") is a fixed, extremely common opener for politely getting someone's attention before a question: 请问，洗手间在哪儿？ (Qǐng wèn, xǐshǒujiān zài nǎr?, "Excuse me, where's the restroom?").

examples.pinyin: Qǐng wèn, nǐ jiào shénme míngzi?

examples.english: Let me treat you to a meal.

chapter: Chapter 12: Quantity and Connectors — 一点儿, 和, 还是
title: 一点儿 — "A Little / A Bit"
theory: 一点儿 (yìdiǎnr, often shortened to 点儿 in casual speech) means "a little/a bit" and attaches after an adjective or verb to soften or quantify it: 便宜一点儿 (piányi yìdiǎnr), "a little cheaper"; 我会说一点儿汉语 (Wǒ huì shuō yìdiǎnr Hànyǔ), "I can speak a little Chinese." Note it comes after the adjective/verb, the reverse of English "a little," which usually comes before.
After a comparative adjective specifically, 一点儿 signals a small difference: 这个大一点儿 (Zhège dà yìdiǎnr), "This one is a little bigger" (implicitly compared to something just mentioned).

Don't confuse 一点儿 (a small quantity of something) with 有一点儿 (yǒu yìdiǎnr, "somewhat/a bit," placed before an adjective to soften a negative-leaning description): 我有一点儿累 (Wǒ yǒu yìdiǎnr lèi), "I'm a little tired." 有一点儿 tends to appear before things the speaker finds mildly undesirable (tired, expensive, difficult), while plain 一点儿 is neutral.
pattern: Adj/V + 一点儿。　·　有一点儿 + Adj。

examples.english: I can speak a little Chinese.
This one is a little cheaper.
Please give me a little water.

chapter: Chapter 12: Quantity and Connectors — 一点儿, 和, 还是
title: Connecting Words — 和 (and) vs. 还是 (or, in questions)
theory: 和 (hé, "and") connects two nouns or noun phrases, not verbs or full clauses — Chinese generally doesn't need a word for "and" between two verbs or sentences the way English does; they're simply placed one after another. 我和他是朋友 (Wǒ hé tā shì péngyou), "He and I are friends." Using 和 to join two full sentences ("I went home and I ate dinner") is not natural in this basic pattern.

还是 (háishi, "or") is used inside a question offering a choice between two options — the sentence is already a genuine A-or-B question, so it never also takes 吗: 你要咖啡还是茶？(Nǐ yào kāfēi háishi chá?, "Do you want coffee or tea?"). Adding 吗 here would be ungrammatical, since the question itself already presents the choice.

或者 (huòzhě, "or") is the word for "or" in a plain statement rather than a question ("I'll go tomorrow or the day after"), and belongs to a later chapter — for now, remember that 还是 specifically marks an either/or question.
pattern: N1 + 和 + N2。　·　A + 还是 + B？

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hé nǐ dōu shì xuéshēng.
examples.english: You and I are both students.
Do you want coffee or tea?

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng qù Běijīng háishi Shànghǎi?
examples.english: Do you want to go to Beijing or Shanghai?

chapter: Chapter 1: Ongoing and Imminent Actions — 在/正在, 着, 快要/就要...了
title: 在/正在 + Verb — Actions in Progress
theory: Placed directly before a verb, 在 (zài) or the fuller 正在 (zhèngzài) marks an action as currently in progress, similar to English "-ing": 我在吃饭 (Wǒ zài chīfàn), "I am eating." This is a different grammatical role from the 在 covered in HSK1 (location), which marked where something is — context (a verb following vs. a place-noun following) tells them apart, and in fact they often appear together: 我在家吃饭 combines both, "I'm at home eating."

正在 is simply a more emphatic, more clearly "right now, in the middle of" version of bare 在: 他正在睡觉 (Tā zhèngzài shuìjiào), "He is (right in the middle of) sleeping." 正 alone (without 在) can also mark progressive aspect in careful/written style, though 在 and 正在 are far more common in speech.

The sentence-final particle 呢 (from HSK1) very often reinforces a progressive-aspect sentence, either alongside 在/正在 or, in casual speech, entirely on its own: 他在睡觉呢 (Tā zài shuìjiào ne) or simply 他睡觉呢 both mean "He's sleeping (right now)." 呢 here signals "this is an ongoing state," distinct from its follow-up-question use.
Negating a progressive action uses 没(有), not 不: 我没在吃饭 (Wǒ méi zài chīfàn), "I'm not eating (right now)" — following the same 没-for-completed/ongoing-actions rule that 了 followed in HSK1.
pattern: S + 在/正在 + V(+O) (+ 呢)。

chapter: Chapter 1: Ongoing and Imminent Actions — 在/正在, 着, 快要/就要...了
title: 着 (zhe) — Durative/Continuous States
theory: While 在 marks an action actively unfolding, 着 (zhe), attached directly after a verb, marks a resulting state that continues to hold — the difference between "is doing" and "is in a state of having done, and that state persists": 门开着 (Mén kāi zhe), "The door is open" (the state of openness persists, from the completed action of opening it) — not "the door is [in the process of] opening."

着 is especially common describing the "backdrop" manner in which another action happens — the first verb+着 sets a continuing posture or state, and a second verb describes what's done during it: 他坐着看书 (Tā zuò zhe kàn shū), "He sits and reads" / "He is reading while sitting," literally "he sitting reads book." The 着-marked verb is the state you're in; the second verb is the actual activity.

着 can combine with 正在 for an action that is both actively ongoing and resulting in a persisting state, especially with verbs describing wearing, holding, or postures: 她正穿着一件红色的衣服 (Tā zhèng chuān zhe yí jiàn hóngsè de yīfu), "She is wearing a red garment (right now)." 穿 (to put on/wear) pairs naturally with 着 because wearing is inherently a continuing state, not a momentary action.
Negation uses 没 + V + 着: 门没开着 (Mén méi kāi zhe), "The door isn't open," though in practice it's more common to simply state the opposite directly (门关着, "the door is closed").

examples.hanzi: 她穿着一件红色的衣服。
examples.pinyin: Tā chuān zhe yí jiàn hóngsè de yīfu.
examples.english: She is wearing a red garment.

examples.pinyin: Qiáng shang guà zhe yì zhāng zhàopiàn.
examples.english: A photo is hanging on the wall.

chapter: Chapter 1: Ongoing and Imminent Actions — 在/正在, 着, 快要/就要...了
title: 快要/就要...了 — About To / On the Verge Of
theory: 快要...了 and 就要...了 both frame an event as imminent — about to happen very soon — bracketing the verb phrase with 快要 or 就要 at the front and the sentence-final 了 (the same "change of state" 了 from HSK1) at the end: 我快要到了 (Wǒ kuàiyào dào le), "I'm about to arrive." The 了 here isn't optional — it's a fixed part of the construction, marking that the imminent event is now close enough to announce.

快 alone (without 要) can also be used the same way in casual speech: 快到了 (Kuài dào le) means the same as 快要到了. 就要 tends to pair more naturally with a specific time word placed before it, emphasizing exactly when the event will happen: 我们下个月就要搬家了 (Wǒmen xià ge yuè jiù yào bānjiā le), "We're moving next month" (the timing is definite and close).

快要 leans toward "any moment now," a purely imminent sense without needing a stated time, while 就要 more comfortably takes a specific near-future time word — but in everyday speech the two overlap heavily and either is often acceptable.
pattern: S + 快(要)/就要 + V(+O) + 了。

examples.english: The movie is about to start.

examples.hanzi: 我们下个月就要搬家了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen xià ge yuè jiù yào bānjiā le.

chapter: Chapter 2: A-not-A Questions — 你去不去, 好不好, 是不是
title: The A-not-A Question Pattern
theory: Beyond adding 吗 (HSK1), Chinese has a second, equally common way to form a yes/no question: state the verb or adjective, then immediately repeat it in its negative form, with no 吗 needed at all — this is called the "A-not-A" pattern. 你去不去？(Nǐ qù bu qù?, "Are you going or not?") uses 去 followed by 不去; 好不好？(Hǎo bu hǎo?, "Is that okay?") uses 好 followed by 不好.

The two forms are functionally equivalent to a 吗-question and are largely interchangeable — 你是学生吗？ and 你是不是学生？ both ask "Are you a student?" — but A-not-A can feel slightly more neutral/genuinely open, while 吗 can sometimes carry a faint expectation toward "yes."

For a two-syllable verb or adjective, the first syllable is often dropped in the negative half to keep the question compact: 喜欢 (xǐhuan, "to like") becomes 喜不喜欢 (xǐ bu xǐhuan), not the longer 喜欢不喜欢 (though the full form is also acceptable and unambiguous).

Just as with 吗, A-not-A cannot be combined with an actual question word (什么/谁/哪/etc.) or with 吗 itself — a sentence is asked one way or the other, never both. 你有没有时间？ from HSK1 is in fact this exact pattern applied to 有: 有 + 没有.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xǐ bu xǐhuan hē chá?

chapter: Chapter 3: Time Clauses — 的时候, 以前, 以后
title: 的时候 — "When..."
theory: 的时候 (de shíhou, literally "the time of...") attaches to the end of a clause (a verb phrase, adjective, or even just a noun) to mean "when [that clause happens/happened]": 吃饭的时候 (chīfàn de shíhou), "when eating." The whole clause-plus-的时候 phrase then functions as a time word and goes before the main verb, following the same word-order rule as all other time expressions from HSK1: 我吃饭的时候看电视 (Wǒ chīfàn de shíhou kàn diànshì), "I watch TV while eating."

的时候 works just as naturally with an adjective or a noun-based description of a life stage as with a verb: 我小的时候 (wǒ xiǎo de shíhou), "when I was young" (小 = young/small, functioning as the "clause"); 学生的时候 (xuésheng de shíhou), "when [I was] a student."

Unlike English "when," 的时候 does not need any tense marking of its own — whether the described time is past, present, or future is understood from context or from other words in the sentence (like 昨天 or 以后), not from 的时候 itself.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ chīfàn de shíhou kàn diànshì.

examples.hanzi: 我小的时候很喜欢画画儿。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎo de shíhou hěn xǐhuan huà huàr.
examples.english: When I was young, I loved drawing.

examples.hanzi: 下雨的时候，我们在家看书。
examples.pinyin: Xià yǔ de shíhou, wǒmen zài jiā kàn shū.
examples.english: When it rains, we read at home.

examples.hanzi: 你来的时候请带一本书。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ lái de shíhou qǐng dài yì běn shū.
examples.english: When you come, please bring a book.

chapter: Chapter 3: Time Clauses — 的时候, 以前, 以后
title: 以前 and 以后 — "Before..." and "After..."
theory: 以前 (yǐqián, "before") and 以后 (yǐhòu, "after") attach to the end of a time word, a duration, or a full verb phrase to establish a before/after relationship: 三点以前 (sān diǎn yǐqián), "before 3 o'clock"; 下课以后 (xiàkè yǐhòu), "after class." As with 的时候, the whole phrase functions as a time word and precedes the main verb: 我下课以后去买东西 (Wǒ xiàkè yǐhòu qù mǎi dōngxi), "I'll go shopping after class."

On their own, without an attached clause, 以前 and 以后 mean simply "before/in the past" and "after this/from now on," referring to the present moment as the implicit reference point: 以前我不会说中文 (Yǐqián wǒ bú huì shuō Zhōngwén), "Before, I couldn't speak Chinese."

A verb phrase before 以前 describes something that has NOT yet happened relative to the reference point, which can feel counterintuitive: 睡觉以前 (shuìjiào yǐqián), "before sleeping," describes an action taken prior to an event that hasn't been marked as complete — no 了 is used on the verb before 以前: 睡觉以前，我看书 (Shuìjiào yǐqián, wǒ kàn shū), "Before sleeping, I read."

后来 (hòulái, "afterward/later on") is related but distinct: unlike 以后, which attaches to a specific clause or time word, 后来 stands alone at the start of a sentence narrating what happened next in a story, purely about sequence in the past: 后来我们成了好朋友 (Hòulái wǒmen chéng le hǎo péngyou), "Afterward, we became good friends."

examples.pinyin: Xiàkè yǐhòu wǒ qù mǎi dōngxi.
Yǐqián wǒ bú huì shuō Zhōngwén.
Hòulái wǒmen chéng le hǎo péngyou.

chapter: Chapter 4: Talking About Experience — 过 (guo)
title: 过 — "Have Ever Done" (Experiential Aspect)
theory: Attached directly after a verb, 过 (guo, neutral tone) marks that an action has been experienced at least once at some unspecified point in the past — the emphasis is on the experience itself having happened, not on when or how many times: 我去过中国 (Wǒ qùguo Zhōngguó), "I've been to China (at some point in my life)."

This is meaningfully different from the completed-action 了 covered in HSK1: 我去了中国 reports a specific, often recent trip as a completed event, while 我去过中国 simply states that the experience of going is part of your history, with no implication about when. The two can combine — 我去过中国三次了 (Wǒ qùguo Zhōngguó sān cì le), "I've been to China three times [so far]" — using 过 for the experience and a trailing 了 to mark this as the current, still-relevant count.

Negation uses 没(有), and 过 stays attached to the verb (unlike completed-action 了, which drops entirely under negation): 我没去过中国 (Wǒ méi qùguo Zhōngguó), "I've never been to China." This is worth contrasting directly with HSK1's 了 rule: 了 disappears when negated, 过 does not.
The question form follows the regular patterns already known: 你去过中国吗？ or the A-not-A form 你去没去过中国？ both ask "Have you ever been to China?"

examples.english: Have you ever eaten Chinese food?

examples.hanzi: 我看过这个电影三次了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ kànguo zhège diànyǐng sān cì le.
examples.english: I've watched this movie three times so far.

chapter: Chapter 5: Separable Verbs (离合词) — 见面, 帮忙, 结婚, 毕业, 生气
title: Separable Verbs — 见面, 帮忙, 结婚, 毕业, 生气, and More
theory: A number of common two-syllable "verbs" in Chinese are actually verb+object compounds fused into a single dictionary word — called 离合词 (líhécí, "separable words"). 见面 (jiànmiàn, "to meet") breaks down as 见 (see) + 面 (face); 帮忙 (bāngmáng, "to help") as 帮 (help) + 忙 (a favor); 结婚 (jiéhūn, "to marry") as 结 (tie/form) + 婚 (marriage); similarly 毕业 (graduate), 生气 (get angry), 睡觉 (sleep), 游泳 (swim), 唱歌 (sing).

Because the second half is grammatically an object, these verbs cannot take a second, separate object directly after them the way an ordinary transitive verb can. You cannot say 见面他 to mean "meet him" — instead, the person must be introduced earlier with 跟 (gēn, "with," from HSK1): 我跟他见面 (Wǒ gēn tā jiànmiàn), "I meet with him." The same applies to 帮忙: not 帮忙我, but 帮我的忙 (bāng wǒ de máng) or simply the plain transitive verb 帮 alone: 帮我 (help me).

Aspect particles — 了, 过, 着 — insert directly between the two halves rather than attaching to the end of the whole compound: 见过面 (jiànguo miàn, "have met [before]"), not 见面过; 见了面 (jiàn le miàn, "met"), not 见面了. This mid-word insertion is the clearest sign that these are really verb+object pairs, not single indivisible verbs.
Quantity/frequency expressions also insert in the middle rather than following the whole word: 见过两次面 (jiànguo liǎng cì miàn), "have met twice," not 见面过两次.
pattern: V + (了/过/着) + O(second half)　·　跟 + Person + V(compound)

examples.pinyin: Nǐ néng bāng wǒ de máng ma?

chapter: Chapter 6: Result Complements — 完, 懂, 到, 见, 错, 好
title: Common Result Complements — 完, 懂, 到, 见
theory: A result complement is a second syllable attached directly after a verb that specifies the outcome the action reached — not just that the action happened, but that it succeeded in a particular way. 完 (wán, "finish") attaches to show an action was carried through to completion: 我吃完了 (Wǒ chī wán le), "I've finished eating" — a more specific claim than plain 我吃了 (Wǒ chī le), "I ate," which says nothing about whether the food was finished.

懂 (dǒng, "understand") attaches after verbs of perception to confirm the perception succeeded in yielding comprehension: 听懂 (tīngdǒng, "listen and understand"), 看懂 (kàndǒng, "read/watch and understand"). 我听懂了 (Wǒ tīngdǒng le), "I understood [what I heard]," is different from just 我听了 (Wǒ tīng le), "I listened" — which says nothing about comprehension.

到 (dào, "arrive/reach") attaches to mark that an action successfully reached its target or goal: 找到 (zhǎodào, "find" — literally "search and reach"), 买到 (mǎidào, "successfully buy/obtain"), 听到/看到 (hear/see — perceiving something, distinct from 听懂/看懂's "and understood it"). 我找到钥匙了 (Wǒ zhǎodào yàoshi le), "I found the keys."

见 (jiàn, "perceive") attaches similarly to verbs of perception, marking that a sensory perception simply registered, with no implication of understanding: 听见 (tīngjiàn, "hear," a sound registering) vs. 听懂 (understood the content) — 我听见了，但没听懂 (Wǒ tīngjiàn le, dàn méi tīngdǒng), "I heard it, but I didn't understand it," captures the exact contrast.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ tīngjiàn le, dàn méi tīngdǒng.
examples.english: I heard it, but I didn't understand it.

chapter: Chapter 6: Result Complements — 完, 懂, 到, 见, 错, 好
title: More Result Complements and Negation — 错, 好, and Negating with 没
theory: 错 (cuò, "wrong/mistaken") attaches after a verb to show the action was carried out, but incorrectly: 写错 (xiěcuò, "write incorrectly"), 说错 (shuōcuò, "misspeak"), 听错 (tīngcuò, "mishear"). 我写错了 (Wǒ xiěcuò le), "I wrote it wrong," focuses on the mistaken action itself.

好 (hǎo) as a result complement (distinct from its ordinary adjective use, "good") marks that an action was completed satisfactorily/properly, ready for use: 准备好 (zhǔnbèi hǎo, "get fully ready"), 做好 (zuòhǎo, "get [it] done properly"), 说好 (shuōhǎo, "settle/agree on [something]"). 我准备好了 (Wǒ zhǔnbèi hǎo le), "I'm all ready."

All result complements — this section's and the previous one's — are negated with 没(有), exactly like completed-action 了 from HSK1, and the complement stays attached while the (usually optional after negation) 了 is dropped: 我没吃完 (Wǒ méi chī wán), "I haven't finished eating" (not 我没吃完了). This mirrors the 了/没 rule you already know — negation removes 了, not the complement.

Because a result complement already builds in an outcome, using 不 instead of 没 shifts the meaning to a general capability/willingness statement rather than a report about a specific event — this overlaps with the Potential Complement pattern (Chapter 8), where 不 is inserted between the verb and result to mean "cannot achieve this result": 我吃不完 (Wǒ chī bu wán), "I can't finish eating [it, there's too much]," is a different sentence from the simple negation 我没吃完 (haven't finished yet).
pattern: V + 错/好 (+ 了)。　·　S + 没 + V + Complement。

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiěcuò le yí ge zì.

examples.english: You said it wrong / You're mistaken.

chapter: Chapter 7: Directional Complements — 来/去 and 上/下/进/出/回/过 + 来/去
title: Simple Directional Complements — 来 and 去
theory: Attached directly after a motion verb, 来 (lái, "come," toward the speaker) and 去 (qù, "go," away from the speaker) specify the direction of the motion relative to the speaker's position — the same directional meaning they have as standalone verbs (HSK1), just now riding on another verb: 进来 (jìnlái, "come in"), 出去 (chūqù, "go out").

If a place is mentioned, it's inserted between the main verb and 来/去, not after: 回家来 (huí jiā lái), "come back home," with 家 (home) sitting between 回 (return) and 来 (toward the speaker). This mirrors the general rule that place phrases sit close to the verb they modify rather than trailing at the very end.

Whether to use 来 or 去 depends entirely on the speaker's (or, in narration, the reference point's) position, not on the action itself: someone calling from inside a house says 进来 (come in) to a person outside, while that same person outside, describing their own action, would say 我要进去 (Wǒ yào jìnqù), "I'm going to go in" — same action, opposite direction word, because the vantage point differs.
pattern: V + 来/去。　·　V + Place + 来/去。

examples.english: I'm going to step out for a bit.

chapter: Chapter 7: Directional Complements — 来/去 and 上/下/进/出/回/过 + 来/去
title: Compound Directional Complements — 上/下/进/出/回/过 + 来/去
theory: The simple directional verbs from HSK1 — 上 (up), 下 (down), 进 (in), 出 (out), 回 (back), 过 (across/over) — can each combine with 来/去 to form a compound directional complement, attached after a main verb, giving a precise two-part picture: which direction relative to the ground/starting point, and which direction relative to the speaker. 拿上来 (ná shànglái), "bring it up (here)"; 走进去 (zǒu jìnqù), "walk in (there)."

This compound complement attaches after a main verb of motion or manner: 走 (walk), 拿 (carry), 跑 (run), 爬 (climb) are all common hosts: 他跑出去了 (Tā pǎo chūqù le), "He ran out." The compound as a whole — 出去 — behaves just like the simple 来/去 from the previous section, just adding the extra layer of 上/下/进/出/回/过.

As with simple directional complements, an object referring to a place is inserted before 来/去 (after the 上/下/进/出/回/过 part): 他走进教室来了 (Tā zǒu jìn jiàoshì lái le), "He walked into the classroom (toward here)," with 教室 (classroom) sitting between 进 and 来.

Many of these compounds have taken on extended, non-literal meanings beyond pure physical direction: 想出来 (xiǎng chūlái, literally "think out"), meaning "figure out/come up with [an idea]," no longer describes physical motion at all.
pattern: V + 上/下/进/出/回/过 + 来/去 + (Place before 来/去)。

examples.english: Please bring the book up here.

examples.pinyin: Tā zǒu jìn jiàoshì lái le.
Wǒ xiǎng chūlái yí ge bànfǎ.

chapter: Chapter 8: The Three "De" Particles — 的, 得, 地, and Potential Complements
title: 的 as a General Attributive Marker (Beyond Possession)
theory: HSK1 introduced 的 for possession (我的书, "my book"). The same particle has a much broader job: attaching almost any descriptive word or phrase to a noun that follows, not just a possessor. A simple adjective: 红色的苹果 (hóngsè de píngguǒ), "the red apple." A phrase describing what something is characterized by: 学中文的学生 (xué Zhōngwén de xuésheng), "students who study Chinese."

Most strikingly, an entire clause can sit in front of 的 to modify a noun, functioning much like an English relative clause ("the book that I bought") but with the structure reversed — the description comes first, then 的, then the noun, with no separate word for "that/which": 我昨天买的书 (wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū), literally "I yesterday bought 的 book," meaning "the book I bought yesterday." This is simply the same possessive-style 的 pattern (X + 的 + Noun) from HSK1, just with X now being a full clause instead of a single possessor noun.

Single-syllable adjectives usually attach directly to the noun without 的 when they form a fixed, tightly-bound description (红花, "red flower"), while a two-syllable or more elaborate description almost always keeps 的: 漂亮的花 (piàoliang de huā), "a beautiful flower." This distinction is a matter of degree rather than a hard rule, and native intuition develops with exposure.

examples.hanzi: 我昨天买的书很有意思。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū hěn yǒu yìsi.
examples.english: The book I bought yesterday is interesting.

examples.hanzi: 那个穿红衣服的人是我朋友。
examples.pinyin: Nàge chuān hóng yīfu de rén shì wǒ péngyou.
examples.english: That person wearing red is my friend.

examples.hanzi: 学中文的学生越来越多。
examples.pinyin: Xué Zhōngwén de xuésheng yuè lái yuè duō.
examples.english: There are more and more students studying Chinese.

chapter: Chapter 8: The Three "De" Particles — 的, 得, 地, and Potential Complements
title: The Degree Complement 得 (de) — V/Adj + 得 + Description
theory: 得 (de, neutral tone — a completely different word from 的, despite sounding identical) attaches directly after a verb or adjective to introduce a description of the degree or manner of that verb/adjective, most often translated with "so...that" or a simple adverb: 他跑得很快 (Tā pǎo de hěn kuài), "He runs fast" (literally "he runs 得 very fast"). 忙得没有时间吃饭 (máng de méiyǒu shíjiān chīfàn), "so busy that there's no time to eat," shows how far the description after 得 can extend, sometimes into a full clause.

Unlike an ordinary adverb placed before the verb, 得 requires the description to come after the verb — this is the structural signal for "this is a degree/manner complement," distinct from every adverb-before-verb pattern seen so far (很, 都, 也, 一起, all from HSK1).

If the verb already has an object, the verb must be repeated before 得 introduces the complement, since 得 always attaches directly to the verb: 他说中文说得很好 (Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo), "He speaks Chinese well" — 说 (speak) appears twice: once with its object 中文, and again immediately before 得. Dropping the object entirely (他说得很好) is also fine when it's already clear from context.
Negation happens inside the complement, after 得, not on the main verb: 他跑得不快 (Tā pǎo de bú kuài), "He doesn't run fast" — not 他不跑得快.

examples.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
Wǒ máng de méiyǒu shíjiān chīfàn.
examples.english: I'm so busy I don't have time to eat.

chapter: Chapter 8: The Three "De" Particles — 的, 得, 地, and Potential Complements
title: Potential Complements — V + 得/不 + Result/Direction
theory: Inserting 得 (de) or 不 (bù) between a verb and a result complement (Chapter 6) or directional complement (Chapter 7) creates a potential complement, stating whether the action is capable of reaching that result — "can/can't [verb] to the point of [result]." 听得懂 (tīng de dǒng), "can understand by listening"; 听不懂 (tīng bu dǒng), "can't understand by listening" — built directly from 听懂 with 得/不 spliced into the middle.

This is structurally distinct from, but easy to confuse with, the plain negation of a result complement (没 + V + Result, e.g. 没听懂, "didn't [end up] understanding"). 没听懂 reports a specific past event's outcome; 听不懂 states a general capability — 我说中文，但是他听不懂 (Wǒ shuō Zhōngwén, dànshì tā tīng bu dǒng), "I speak Chinese, but he can't understand it," describes an ongoing inability, not a one-time failure.

The same 得/不 insertion works with directional complements: 上得去 (shàng de qù, "can go up") and 上不去 (shàng bu qù, "can't go up") — e.g. 箱子太重，我拿不上去 (Xiāngzi tài zhòng, wǒ ná bu shàngqù), "The box is too heavy, I can't carry it up."

A small number of potential complements are frozen, very common expressions worth learning as set phrases: 来得及 (lái de jí, "there's still time / can make it in time") and 来不及 (lái bu jí, "there's no time left / too late") are best learned directly as a pair rather than derived from an independently common result complement.

examples.hanzi: 我说中文，但是他听不懂。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ shuō Zhōngwén, dànshì tā tīng bu dǒng.
examples.english: I speak Chinese, but he can't understand it.

examples.pinyin: Xiāngzi tài zhòng, wǒ ná bu shàngqù.
examples.english: The box is too heavy, I can't carry it up.

chapter: Chapter 8: The Three "De" Particles — 的, 得, 地, and Potential Complements
title: 地 — Marking Adverbials Before a Verb (的 vs 得 vs 地 Recap)
theory: 地 (de, neutral tone — the third identically-pronounced "de," after 的 and 得) attaches after a descriptive word — almost always a two-syllable adjective or a phrase — to turn it into an adverbial modifying the verb that follows: 高兴地说 (gāoxìng de shuō), "said happily," 认真地学习 (rènzhēn de xuéxí), "study seriously." Unlike 得's degree complement, which describes the verb from after it, 地 always sits before the verb it modifies.

Only descriptive words substantial enough to carry real manner-meaning typically take 地 — most single-syllable adjectives skip it and simply sit before the verb bare, the same way 很 + adjective sentences work as predicates (HSK1): 快走 (kuài zǒu, "walk quickly") rather than 快地走. Two-syllable and more elaborate descriptions almost always keep 地: 慢慢地走 (mànmàn de zǒu), "walk slowly."

With all three "de" particles now introduced, here's the full contrast in one place: 的 attaches a description to a following NOUN (漂亮的花, "a beautiful flower"); 地 attaches a description to a following VERB, describing how the action is done (慢慢地走, "walk slowly"); 得 attaches after a verb/adjective to describe the resulting degree or manner (走得很慢, "walks so slowly," describing the walking after the fact). All three are unstressed and pronounced identically as "de" in speech — only the character written, and its position relative to the verb, distinguishes them.

examples.hanzi: 孩子们高兴地跑出去玩儿。
examples.pinyin: Háizimen gāoxìng de pǎo chūqù wánr.
examples.english: The children ran out happily to play.

chapter: Chapter 9: The 把 and 被 Constructions
title: 把 (bǎ) — Disposal/Handling Construction
theory: In an ordinary sentence, the object follows the verb (我吃了苹果, "I ate the apple"). The 把 construction moves the object in front of the verb instead, introduced by 把: 我把苹果吃了 (Wǒ bǎ píngguǒ chī le), same core meaning, but shifting emphasis onto what specifically happened to that object.

A bare 把 sentence with nothing after the verb is not grammatical — the verb almost always needs a complement of some kind following it: a result complement (把苹果吃完, "eat the apple all the way"), a directional complement (把书拿过来, "bring the book over"), 了 (把苹果吃了), or a location (把书放在桌子上, "put the book on the table"). This — something must follow the verb — is the single most important rule of the 把 construction.

把 is used specifically when the object is something specific and already known/identifiable to the listener (definite), never a brand-new, unspecified thing being introduced for the first time — you'd say 我买了一本书 (I bought a book — new information) but never 我把一本书买了 with an indefinite "a book." 把 practically requires "the," not "a," in the English translation.

Negation and modal verbs go before 把, not between 把 and the object: 我没把作业做完 (Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán), "I didn't finish the homework," 我要把这个问题解决 (Wǒ yào bǎ zhège wèntí jiějué), "I want to resolve this problem."

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shang.
examples.english: Please put the book on the table.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuò wán le.
Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.

chapter: Chapter 9: The 把 and 被 Constructions
title: 被 (bèi) — The Passive Construction
theory: 被 (bèi) marks a passive sentence, where the subject is the one something happened TO, rather than the one doing the action — the doer (if mentioned) follows 被: 杯子被他打破了 (Bēizi bèi tā dǎpò le), "The cup was broken by him." The doer can be omitted when unknown or unimportant: 杯子被打破了 (Bēizi bèi dǎpò le), "The cup got broken."

Just like 把 sentences, a 被 sentence's verb almost always needs something following it — a result complement, 了, or similar — a bare verb with nothing after it sounds incomplete: 杯子被打破了 works because 破 (broken) is a result complement on 打 (hit/strike); a bare 杯子被打 sounds unfinished.

被 sentences are used far less often than passive voice in English — Chinese generally prefers describing events with an active subject whenever the doer is known, and reserves 被 specifically for situations with a genuinely negative or unfortunate outcome for the subject: 杯子被打破了 (something bad happened to the cup) is natural, while a neutral, positive, or engineered-sounding passive would usually be rephrased with an active subject instead of forced into 被.

让 (ràng) and 叫 (jiào) can substitute for 被 in casual speech with a similar passive-ish "make/let X happen to someone" sense, though they're better understood as separate causative verbs that happen to overlap with 被's territory rather than true synonyms — worth noting for recognition, without needing to master the distinction in depth yet.

examples.english: The cup was broken by him.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.
Zhè běn shū bèi jiè zǒu le.
examples.english: This book has been borrowed (taken out).
The cake was eaten by him.

chapter: Chapter 10: Coverbs — 给 and 对
title: 给 (gěi) and 对 (duì) — Marking the Beneficiary and Target of an Action
theory: 给 (gěi) as a coverb (a word that acts like a preposition, placed before the verb) marks who an action is done for or directed to — the beneficiary or recipient: 我给你打电话 (Wǒ gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà), "I'll call you" (literally "for/to you make-call"). This is distinct from 给's plain verb use, "to give" (我给你一本书, "I give you a book," where 给 itself is the main verb).

Many everyday actions naturally take a 给-phrase to specify who benefits: 给我买 (gěi wǒ mǎi, "buy [it] for me"), 给他写信 (gěi tā xiě xìn, "write him a letter"), 给妈妈打电话 (gěi māma dǎ diànhuà, "call mom"). The 给-phrase, like every coverb phrase, goes before the main verb, following the same word-order rule established for 在 and 从...到... in HSK1.

对 (duì) as a coverb marks the target or direction of an attitude, statement, or effect — roughly "toward/regarding": 对我说 (duì wǒ shuō, "say to me"), 他对中国历史很感兴趣 (Tā duì Zhōngguó lìshǐ hěn gǎn xìngqù), "He's very interested in Chinese history." 对 also appears in the common evaluative pattern 对身体好/不好 (duì shēntǐ hǎo/bù hǎo), "good/bad for one's health."

The core difference: 给 marks who receives the benefit or result of an action (a person actively affected, often the indirect object of a verb like give/call/write/buy), while 对 marks the target of an attitude, feeling, statement, or effect (often not directly "receiving" anything, just being the topic something is oriented toward).

examples.hanzi: 他对中国历史很感兴趣。
examples.pinyin: Tā duì Zhōngguó lìshǐ hěn gǎn xìngqù.
examples.english: He's very interested in Chinese history.
Exercise is good for your health.

chapter: Chapter 11: Comparisons and Degree — 比, 没有, 一样, 越来越, 极了
title: Basic 比 Comparisons (including 更/还)
theory: 比 (bǐ) compares two things directly, with the structure A + 比 + B + Adjective, meaning "A is more [adjective] than B": 他比我高 (Tā bǐ wǒ gāo), "He is taller than me." 很 is dropped in a 比 sentence — a bare adjective is enough, since 比 itself already establishes the comparison; adding 很 back in (他比我很高) is a common but incorrect beginner habit.

To specify by how much, a quantity follows the adjective: 他比我高五公分 (Tā bǐ wǒ gāo wǔ gōngfēn), "He is 5 centimeters taller than me." 一点儿 (HSK1) and 得多 work here to mean "a little more" and "a lot more": 他比我高一点儿 (a little taller), 他比我高得多 (much taller).

更 (gèng) or 还 (hái) can be inserted directly before the adjective to mean "even more" — useful when comparing within an already-established comparison: 他很高，但是他哥哥更高 (Tā hěn gāo, dànshì tā gēge gèng gāo), "He's tall, but his older brother is even taller." Unlike plain 比 sentences, 更/还 here doesn't require an explicit 比-phrase.

Negating a 比 sentence uses 不比, but be careful: 他不比我高 does NOT simply mean "he's shorter than me" — it means "he's not [necessarily] taller than me," a weaker claim that leaves open whether they're the same height. To directly state "less than," Chinese generally prefers the 没有 pattern from the next section.
pattern: A + 比 + B + Adj (+ Amount)。　·　A + 更/还 + Adj。

examples.pinyin: Tā bǐ wǒ gāo wǔ gōngfēn.
examples.english: He is 5 cm taller than me.

examples.hanzi: 他很高，但是他哥哥更高。
examples.pinyin: Tā hěn gāo, dànshì tā gēge gèng gāo.
examples.english: He's tall, but his older brother is even taller.
Today is a little colder than yesterday.

chapter: Chapter 11: Comparisons and Degree — 比, 没有, 一样, 越来越, 极了
title: 没有 and 一样 — "Not As...As" and "The Same As"
theory: 没有 (méiyǒu) used between two things being compared, followed by an adjective, means "A doesn't reach/measure up to B in [adjective]-ness" — the natural way to say "A is not as [adjective] as B," and the most common way to express the logical opposite of a 比 sentence: 我没有他高 (Wǒ méiyǒu tā gāo), "I'm not as tall as he is." This is the same 没有 word from HSK1 (possession/existence) doing a new job here.

跟...一样 (gēn...yíyàng) states that two things are equal/the same in some respect: 我跟他一样高 (Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo), "I'm the same height as him." 一样 alone, without a following adjective, simply asserts sameness in general: 这两个一样 (Zhè liǎng ge yíyàng), "These two are the same."

Negating 一样 with 不一样 states a plain difference without specifying direction: 我跟他不一样高 (Wǒ gēn tā bù yíyàng gāo), "I'm not the same height as him" (could be taller or shorter — unlike 没有, which specifically claims "less than").
Between these three tools — 比 (X is more than Y), 没有 (X is not as much as Y), 跟...一样 (X equals Y) — a learner now has a complete toolkit for any comparison.
pattern: A + 没有 + B + Adj。　·　A + 跟 + B + (不)一样 (+ Adj)。

examples.english: I'm not as tall as he is.
Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
I'm the same height as him.

examples.pinyin: Zhè liǎng jiàn yīfu bù yíyàng.
examples.english: These two garments aren't the same.

chapter: Chapter 11: Comparisons and Degree — 比, 没有, 一样, 越来越, 极了
title: 越来越 and 越...越... — "More and More" / "The More...The More..."
theory: 越来越 (yuè lái yuè) placed directly before an adjective or verb describes a quality that keeps intensifying over time, "more and more ___": 天气越来越冷 (Tiānqì yuè lái yuè lěng), "The weather is getting colder and colder." The whole four-character sequence functions as a single fixed expression meaning "increasingly."

The more general pattern 越 A 越 B links two clauses so that increasing A causes or accompanies increasing B, "the more..., the more...": 越吃越想吃 (yuè chī yuè xiǎng chī), "the more you eat, the more you want to eat"; 你越解释，我越不懂 (Nǐ yuè jiěshì, wǒ yuè bù dǒng), "The more you explain, the less I understand" — 越 can pair with a negative just as naturally as a positive.

越来越 is really a special case of this same 越...越... pattern, where the first half is fixed as 来 (roughly, "as time comes/goes on") rather than a specific described action — that's why 越来越 always describes something changing over time, while 越A越B can link any two related actions or qualities.
pattern: S + 越来越 + Adj/V。　·　越 + A + 越 + B。

examples.english: The weather is getting colder and colder.

examples.pinyin: Tā de Zhōngwén yuè lái yuè hǎo.
examples.english: His Chinese is getting better and better.
The more you eat, the more you want to eat.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yuè jiěshì, wǒ yuè bù dǒng.
examples.english: The more you explain, the less I understand.

chapter: Chapter 11: Comparisons and Degree — 比, 没有, 一样, 越来越, 极了
title: 极了 — "Extremely ___"
theory: 极了 (jíle) attaches directly after an adjective to intensify it to an extreme degree, "extremely/incredibly ___": 好极了 (hǎo jíle), "great!/extremely good." This closely parallels 太...了 from HSK1 — both wrap an adjective with a fixed 了 at the end — but 极了 attaches only at the end and generally carries a more purely enthusiastic/exclamatory feel, without 太's frequent undertone of "more than desirable."

极了 is used almost exclusively with positive or emphatic exclamations in everyday speech — 好极了！(great!), 漂亮极了 (gorgeous), 高兴极了 (thrilled) — and doesn't combine naturally with mundane, low-key adjectives the way 很 does.

A closely related, more casual/colloquial intensifier is 死了 (sǐle, literally "died"), attached the same way after an adjective, often for a complaint rather than a compliment: 累死了 (lèi sǐle), "dead tired," 热死了 (rè sǐle), "unbearably hot." Despite the dramatic literal meaning, this is purely a figure of speech.

examples.hanzi: 听到这个消息，我高兴极了。
examples.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, wǒ gāoxìng jíle.
examples.english: I was thrilled to hear this news.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 虽然...但是 — Although...But
theory: 虽然 (suīrán, "although") opens the first clause and 但是 (dànshì, "but") opens the second, together framing a contrast between an expected implication and what actually happens: 虽然天气很冷，但是我们还是出去了 (Suīrán tiānqì hěn lěng, dànshì wǒmen háishi chūqù le), "Although the weather was cold, we still went out." Unlike English, where using both "although" and "but" is considered redundant, Chinese requires both halves — dropping 但是 and using only 虽然 sounds incomplete.
可是 (kěshì) can substitute for 但是 with essentially the same meaning and function, a matter of style rather than grammar — 可是 tends to feel very slightly more conversational.

虽然 can move to the very start of the sentence or sit right after its own subject, whichever subject it belongs to: 他虽然很忙，但是每天都运动 (Tā suīrán hěn máng, dànshì měitiān dōu yùndòng), "Although he's busy, he exercises every day" — 虽然 here follows 他 because 他 is specifically the subject of the 虽然-clause.
pattern: 虽然 + A，但是/可是 + B。

examples.hanzi: 虽然天气很冷，但是我们还是出去了。
examples.pinyin: Suīrán tiānqì hěn lěng, dànshì wǒmen háishi chūqù le.
examples.english: Although the weather was cold, we still went out.

examples.hanzi: 他虽然很忙，但是每天都运动。
examples.pinyin: Tā suīrán hěn máng, dànshì měitiān dōu yùndòng.
examples.english: Although he's busy, he exercises every day.

examples.hanzi: 这个东西虽然贵，但是很好用。
examples.pinyin: Zhège dōngxi suīrán guì, dànshì hěn hǎoyòng.
examples.english: Although this thing is expensive, it's very useful.

examples.hanzi: 虽然我不会说中文，可是我听得懂。
examples.pinyin: Suīrán wǒ bú huì shuō Zhōngwén, kěshì wǒ tīng de dǒng.
examples.english: Although I can't speak Chinese, I can understand it.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 因为...所以 — Because...So
theory: 因为 (yīnwèi, "because") introduces the reason, and 所以 (suǒyǐ, "so/therefore") introduces the result — again, unlike English, Chinese comfortably uses both together in one sentence: 因为下雨，所以我们没去公园 (Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒmen méi qù gōngyuán), "Because it rained, we didn't go to the park."

Either half can be dropped when the sentence structure or context already makes the logic clear. In casual speech, 因为 alone frequently answers a "why" question on its own, with 所以 simply unnecessary: A: 你为什么不去？B: 因为我很忙 (Yīnwèi wǒ hěn máng), "Because I'm busy."

Word order is flexible in one specific way: the 因为-clause doesn't have to come first. 我们没去公园，因为下雨 (result first, reason second) is equally natural — but if both halves appear, 所以 must still directly precede the result clause.

examples.hanzi: 因为下雨，所以我们没去公园。
examples.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒmen méi qù gōngyuán.
examples.english: Because it rained, we didn't go to the park.

examples.hanzi: 我很累，因为昨天没睡好。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ hěn lèi, yīnwèi zuótiān méi shuì hǎo.
examples.english: I'm tired because I didn't sleep well last night.

examples.hanzi: A: 你为什么不去？B: 因为我很忙。
examples.pinyin: A: Nǐ wèishénme bú qù? B: Yīnwèi wǒ hěn máng.
examples.english: A: Why aren't you going? B: Because I'm busy.

examples.hanzi: 因为他会说中文，所以公司请他去中国工作。
examples.pinyin: Yīnwèi tā huì shuō Zhōngwén, suǒyǐ gōngsī qǐng tā qù Zhōngguó gōngzuò.
examples.english: Because he can speak Chinese, the company sent him to work in China.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 如果...就 — If...Then
theory: 如果 (rúguǒ, "if") introduces a condition, and 就 (jiù, "then") introduces what follows from it: 如果明天下雨，我们就不去了 (Rúguǒ míngtiān xià yǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù le), "If it rains tomorrow, then we won't go." 就 sits directly before the verb of the second clause, after its own subject — the same position adverbs like 也/都 (HSK1) occupy.

如果 can be dropped in casual speech when context makes clear a condition is being stated, leaving just the 就-clause to carry the "then" meaning, though keeping 如果 is always safe and unambiguous, especially in writing.

的话 (dehuà) can optionally follow the condition clause for extra clarity/emphasis, especially useful when 如果 itself is dropped: 明天下雨的话，我们就不去了 (Míngtiān xià yǔ dehuà, wǒmen jiù bú qù le), same meaning. 如果 and 的话 can also be used together: 如果明天下雨的话，...

examples.hanzi: 如果明天下雨，我们就不去了。
examples.pinyin: Rúguǒ míngtiān xià yǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù le.
examples.english: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.

examples.hanzi: 如果你有时间，就来我家玩儿吧。
examples.pinyin: Rúguǒ nǐ yǒu shíjiān, jiù lái wǒ jiā wánr ba.
examples.english: If you have time, come over to my place.

examples.hanzi: 你不喜欢的话，就不要买。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ bù xǐhuan dehuà, jiù búyào mǎi.
examples.english: If you don't like it, don't buy it.

examples.hanzi: 如果没有问题的话，我们就开始吧。
examples.pinyin: Rúguǒ méiyǒu wèntí dehuà, wǒmen jiù kāishǐ ba.
examples.english: If there are no questions, let's begin.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 不但...而且 — Not Only...But Also
theory: 不但 (búdàn, "not only") introduces the first, lesser point, and 而且 (érqiě, "but also/moreover") introduces a second, often stronger point about the same subject: 他不但会说中文，而且说得很好 (Tā búdàn huì shuō Zhōngwén, érqiě shuō de hěn hǎo), "He can not only speak Chinese, but also speaks it well." Both halves build toward a stronger overall statement, unlike 虽然...但是, which sets up a contrast.

也 or 都 (HSK1) very often appears in the 而且 clause to reinforce the additive sense: 这个饭馆不但便宜，而且也很好吃 (Zhège fànguǎn búdàn piányi, érqiě yě hěn hǎochī), "This restaurant is not only cheap, but also delicious." Adding 也/都 isn't required, but it's extremely common.

When the subject is the same across both clauses, 不但 typically comes after the subject. If the two clauses have different subjects, 不但 moves to the very front of the sentence instead: 不但他喜欢，我也喜欢 (Búdàn tā xǐhuan, wǒ yě xǐhuan), "Not only does he like it, I do too."
pattern: 不但 + A，而且(也/都) + B。

examples.hanzi: 他不但会说中文，而且说得很好。
examples.pinyin: Tā búdàn huì shuō Zhōngwén, érqiě shuō de hěn hǎo.
examples.english: He can not only speak Chinese, but speaks it well.

examples.hanzi: 这个饭馆不但便宜，而且很好吃。
examples.pinyin: Zhège fànguǎn búdàn piányi, érqiě hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: This restaurant is not only cheap, but delicious.

examples.pinyin: Búdàn tā xǐhuan, wǒ yě xǐhuan.
examples.english: Not only does he like it, I do too.

examples.hanzi: 她不但漂亮，而且很聪明。
examples.pinyin: Tā búdàn piàoliang, érqiě hěn cōngming.
examples.english: She's not only pretty, but also very smart.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 一边...一边... and 先...然后... — Simultaneous and Sequential Actions
