theory: 一边 A 一边 B (yìbiān A yìbiān B), with a verb phrase in each slot, describes two actions happening at the same time, done by the same person: 他一边吃饭一边看电视 (Tā yìbiān chīfàn yìbiān kàn diànshì), "He eats while watching TV." Both 一边's are required — using only one sounds incomplete.

先 A 然后 B (xiān A rán hòu B) describes two actions in sequence — first one, then the other: 我们先吃饭，然后去看电影 (Wǒmen xiān chīfàn, ránhòu qù kàn diànyǐng), "We'll eat first, then go watch a movie." 然后 can also link more than two steps in a longer sequence.
The key distinction: 一边...一边... requires true simultaneity by a single subject, while 先...然后... is strictly sequential — one action clearly finishes (or at least starts) before the next begins.
pattern: 一边 + V1，一边 + V2。　·　先 + V1，然后 + V2。

examples.hanzi: 他一边吃饭一边看电视。
examples.pinyin: Tā yìbiān chīfàn yìbiān kàn diànshì.

examples.hanzi: 我们先吃饭，然后去看电影。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen xiān chīfàn, ránhòu qù kàn diànyǐng.
examples.english: We'll eat first, then go watch a movie.

examples.hanzi: 先做作业，然后才能玩儿。
examples.pinyin: Xiān zuò zuòyè, ránhòu cái néng wánr.
examples.english: Do your homework first, then you can play.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 除了...以外 — Besides/Except
theory: 除了 A 以外 (chúle A yǐwài) has two distinct meanings depending on what follows in the second clause. When the second clause continues with 还 (hái) or 也 (yě), the meaning is additive, "besides A, also...": 除了英语以外，他还会说法语 (Chúle Yīngyǔ yǐwài, tā hái huì shuō Fǎyǔ), "Besides English, he can also speak French" (he speaks both).

When the second clause instead uses 都 (dōu), the meaning flips to exclusive, "except for A, all...": 除了他以外，我们都去了 (Chúle tā yǐwài, wǒmen dōu qù le), "Except for him, we all went" (everyone but him went). Getting 还/也 vs. 都 right is what determines whether A is included in or excluded from the group being discussed.
以外 is frequently dropped in casual speech, leaving bare 除了, with the meaning unaffected: 除了他，我们都去了 works the same as the fuller version above.
pattern: 除了 + A + 以外，还/也 + B。(additive)　·　除了 + A + 以外，都 + B。(exclusive)

examples.hanzi: 除了英语以外，他还会说法语。
examples.pinyin: Chúle Yīngyǔ yǐwài, tā hái huì shuō Fǎyǔ.
examples.english: Besides English, he can also speak French.

examples.hanzi: 除了他以外，我们都去了。
examples.pinyin: Chúle tā yǐwài, wǒmen dōu qù le.
examples.english: Except for him, we all went.

examples.hanzi: 除了苹果，我什么水果都喜欢吃。
examples.pinyin: Chúle píngguǒ, wǒ shénme shuǐguǒ dōu xǐhuan chī.
examples.english: Except for apples, I like eating any fruit.

examples.hanzi: 除了周末以外，他每天都上班。
examples.pinyin: Chúle zhōumò yǐwài, tā měitiān dōu shàngbān.
examples.english: Except on weekends, he works every day.

chapter: Chapter 12: Complex Sentences and Connectors — 虽然...但是, 因为...所以, 如果...就, 不但...而且, 一边...一边, 除了...以外, 一...就...
title: 一...就... — As Soon As...Then...
theory: 一 A 就 B links two actions so that B follows immediately, automatically, upon A happening: 我一到家就打电话给你 (Wǒ yí dào jiā jiù dǎ diànhuà gěi nǐ), "As soon as I get home, I'll call you." This pattern reuses 就 in essentially the same "right away, promptly" sense it carries elsewhere.

Because B follows so tightly and automatically from A, this pattern is often used for habits or near-automatic reactions, not just one-off plans: 他一喝咖啡就睡不着 (Tā yì hē kāfēi jiù shuì bu zháo), "Whenever he drinks coffee, he can't fall asleep" — describing a reliable pattern, not a single incident.

The subject of both clauses is usually the same person, and appears only once, before 一: 我一到家就打电话 (not 我一到家，我就打电话). When the two clauses have different subjects, each subject appears in its own clause: 老师一进教室，学生就安静了 (Lǎoshī yí jìn jiàoshì, xuésheng jiù ānjìng le), "As soon as the teacher entered the classroom, the students quieted down."

examples.hanzi: 我一到家就打电话给你。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ yí dào jiā jiù dǎ diànhuà gěi nǐ.
examples.english: As soon as I get home, I'll call you.

examples.pinyin: Tā yì hē kāfēi jiù shuì bu zháo.
examples.english: Whenever he drinks coffee, he can't fall asleep.

examples.hanzi: 老师一进教室，学生就安静了。
examples.pinyin: Lǎoshī yí jìn jiàoshì, xuésheng jiù ānjìng le.
examples.english: As soon as the teacher entered, the students quieted down.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yí kàn jiù dǒng le.
examples.english: I understood as soon as I looked at it.

chapter: Chapter 13: 是...的 — Emphasizing Time, Place, or Manner
title: 是...的 Construction
theory: When talking about a specific past action that both speaker and listener already know happened, 是...的 shifts the focus from whether it happened (already assumed) to a specific detail about it — usually when, where, how, or with whom: 我是昨天来的 (Wǒ shì zuótiān lái de), "It was yesterday that I came" (as opposed to plain 我昨天来了, which simply reports that I came yesterday, without special emphasis).

是 sits before the detail being emphasized, and 的 caps off the end of the sentence: 我是坐飞机来的 (Wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de), "I came by plane" (emphasizing the means); 我是在北京出生的 (Wǒ shì zài Běijīng chūshēng de), "I was born in Beijing" (emphasizing the place). 是 is frequently dropped in casual speech while 的 always stays: 我昨天来的 works just as well.

This construction is reserved for actions already completed and already established as fact, and is incompatible with 了 in the same clause. Compare with the completed-action 了 from HSK1: 我去了北京 simply reports a trip happened; 我是去年去北京的 (Wǒ shì qùnián qù Běijīng de) reports the same trip, but with "last year" as the specific piece of information being highlighted, presupposing the listener already knows the trip happened.
Negation places 不是 at the front, and 的 stays at the end: 我不是坐飞机来的，是坐火车来的 (Wǒ bú shì zuò fēijī lái de, shì zuò huǒchē lái de), "I didn't come by plane, I came by train."

examples.english: It was yesterday that I came.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de.
Wǒ shì zài Běijīng chūshēng de.

examples.hanzi: 我不是坐飞机来的，是坐火车来的。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ bú shì zuò fēijī lái de, shì zuò huǒchē lái de.
examples.english: I didn't come by plane, I came by train.

chapter: Chapter 14: Frequency, Duration, and Timing Words — 次/遍, Verb+Duration, 又/再, 才/就, 还
title: 次 and 遍 — Measure Words for Actions
theory: Just as nouns need a measure word when counted (HSK1), actions need one too when counting how many times they occur. 次 (cì) is the general, all-purpose measure word for occurrences of an action: 我去过两次中国 (Wǒ qùguo liǎng cì Zhōngguó), "I've been to China twice." It attaches after the verb (and after any experiential/completed aspect marker like 过 or 了).

遍 (biàn) is a more specific measure word meaning "one complete pass/repetition from start to finish," used especially for reading, watching, or listening to something in its entirety: 我看了三遍这本书 (Wǒ kàn le sān biàn zhè běn shū), "I've read this book three times [cover to cover]." 次 could also be used here more generally, but 遍 specifically emphasizes each pass was complete.

When the object is a pronoun, the frequency phrase goes between the verb and the object: 我见过他两次 (Wǒ jiànguo tā liǎng cì), "I've met him twice." When the object is a longer/more specific noun phrase, the frequency phrase more naturally comes right after the verb, before the object.
Recall from Chapter 5 that with a separable verb (离合词), the frequency phrase inserts into the middle of the compound rather than trailing the whole word: 见过两次面 (jiànguo liǎng cì miàn), not 见面过两次.
pattern: V (+过/了) + Number + 次/遍 (+ O)。

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kàn le sān biàn zhè běn shū.
examples.english: I've read this book three times.
Please say it again (once more, in full).

chapter: Chapter 14: Frequency, Duration, and Timing Words — 次/遍, Verb+Duration, 又/再, 才/就, 还
title: Verb + Duration — Stating How Long
theory: To state how long an action lasted, a duration phrase (a length of time — 三年, 两个小时, 半天, etc.) follows directly after the verb, in the same slot occupied by 次/遍 in the previous section: 我学了三年中文 (Wǒ xué le sān nián Zhōngwén), "I studied Chinese for three years." If there's a specific noun object, the duration typically comes right after the verb and before the object, though repeating the verb (我学中文学了三年) is equally natural and sometimes clearer.

A completed, closed-off duration uses 了 only after the verb, as above. To describe a duration that started in the past and is STILL continuing right now, a second 了 is added at the very end of the sentence: 我学中文学了三年了 (Wǒ xué Zhōngwén xué le sān nián le), "I've been studying Chinese for three years [and I still am]." The trailing 了 here is the same sentence-final "still relevant now" 了 from HSK1.

For a duration referring to a gap since something last happened, the duration phrase moves to before the verb instead, often paired with 没: 我三年没去中国了 (Wǒ sān nián méi qù Zhōngguó le), "I haven't been to China in three years" — the duration here measures the gap since the last occurrence, not how long the going-to-China itself lasted.
pattern: V + 了 + Duration + (了)。　·　Duration + 没 + V + 了。

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xué le sān nián Zhōngwén.
examples.english: I studied Chinese for three years.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xué Zhōngwén xué le sān nián le.
examples.english: I've been studying Chinese for three years (and counting).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ sān nián méi qù Zhōngguó le.
examples.english: I haven't been to China in three years.

examples.pinyin: Tā shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí.

chapter: Chapter 14: Frequency, Duration, and Timing Words — 次/遍, Verb+Duration, 又/再, 才/就, 还
title: 又 vs. 再 — Repetition: Already Happened vs. Will Happen
theory: Both 又 (yòu) and 再 (zài) mean "again," but they split cleanly along one line: 又 is for a repetition that has already happened, and 再 is for a repetition that is still to come: 他昨天来了，今天又来了 (Tā zuótiān lái le, jīntiān yòu lái le), "He came yesterday, and came again today" [already happened] vs. 他今天没来，希望他明天再来 (Tā jīntiān méi lái, xīwàng tā míngtiān zài lái), "He didn't come today, I hope he comes again tomorrow" [not yet happened].

再 is the natural choice in requests, invitations, and anything not yet realized: 请再说一遍 (Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn), "Please say it again" (the repetition hasn't happened yet). 又 would sound wrong here, since nothing has actually recurred yet.

A useful shortcut: 又 pairs naturally with 了 (since it reports something that already came to pass — 又...了), while 再 essentially never takes 了 in the same clause, since by definition it refers to something that hasn't happened yet.
pattern: [Already happened] + 又 + V + 了。　·　[Not yet happened] + 再 + V。

examples.hanzi: 他昨天来了，今天又来了。
examples.pinyin: Tā zuótiān lái le, jīntiān yòu lái le.
examples.english: He came yesterday, and came again today.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ míngtiān zài lái zhǎo nǐ.
examples.english: I'll come find you again tomorrow.

chapter: Chapter 14: Frequency, Duration, and Timing Words — 次/遍, Verb+Duration, 又/再, 才/就, 还
title: 才 vs. 就 — Later Than Expected vs. Sooner Than Expected
theory: 才 (cái) and 就 (jiù), both placed directly before the verb, mark whether an event happened later than expected (才) or sooner/more readily than expected (就) — the speaker's sense of "that's late" or "that's fast," relative to some expectation, not an objective fact about the clock. 他九点才来 (Tā jiǔ diǎn cái lái), "He didn't come until 9" (implying that's later than he should have). 他八点就来了 (Tā bā diǎn jiù lái le), "He came at 8 already" (implying that's early/prompt).

This is the same 就 introduced in this level's 就要...了 (Chapter 1) and 一...就... (Chapter 12) — all three uses share the underlying sense of "right away, promptly, sooner than you'd think." 才, by contrast, specifically signals delay or a higher-than-expected bar being met later than hoped.

A subtle but important rule: a sentence ending in 才 + Verb generally does NOT take a sentence-final 了, even though the event is completed — 他九点才来 is complete as is, not 他九点才来了. 就, on the other hand, very naturally takes 了: 他八点就来了. This asymmetry is a fixed feature of the two words worth memorizing directly.
pattern: [Later than expected] + 才 + V。　·　[Sooner than expected] + 就 + V (+ 了)。

examples.english: He didn't come until 9 (later than expected).

examples.pinyin: Tā bā diǎn jiù lái le.
examples.english: He already came at 8 (earlier than expected).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān hěn wǎn cái shuìjiào.
examples.english: I didn't go to sleep until very late yesterday.

examples.hanzi: 他学了一年就会说中文了。
examples.pinyin: Tā xué le yì nián jiù huì shuō Zhōngwén le.
examples.english: After only a year of studying, he could already speak Chinese.

chapter: Chapter 14: Frequency, Duration, and Timing Words — 次/遍, Verb+Duration, 又/再, 才/就, 还
title: 还 (hái) — Still, Also, and 还没
theory: 还 (hái), placed before the verb like other adverbs already covered, most commonly means "still" — a state or action that continues to hold, unchanged from before: 他还在睡觉 (Tā hái zài shuìjiào), "He's still sleeping." Combined with 没 specifically, 还没 means "still haven't/not yet," pointedly noting that something expected hasn't happened yet, distinct from a plain, neutral 没: 我还没吃饭 (Wǒ hái méi chīfàn), "I haven't eaten yet," implies eating is expected/coming.

还 also means "also/in addition," layering on an extra item, distinct from 也 (HSK1) in one key way: 也 says "this applies too, the same as something else already mentioned," while 还 introduces something additional/extra: 我要一杯咖啡，还要一个面包 (Wǒ yào yì bēi kāfēi, hái yào yí ge miànbāo), "I'd like a coffee, and I'd also like a piece of bread."
还 shows up as part of a few constructions already introduced — 不但...而且还... and the "even more" sense of 还 alongside 更 — all sharing this same core "additionally/beyond what's already true" flavor.

examples.hanzi: 我要一杯咖啡，还要一个面包。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào yì bēi kāfēi, hái yào yí ge miànbāo.
examples.english: I'd like a coffee, and also a piece of bread.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ hái méi zuò wán zuòyè ma?
examples.english: You still haven't finished your homework?

chapter: Chapter 14: Frequency, Duration, and Timing Words — 次/遍, Verb+Duration, 又/再, 才/就, 还
title: Common Noun Measure Words Beyond 个
theory: HSK1 introduced 个 as the universal, default measure word. HSK2 rounds out the set with several more specific measure words, each tied to properties of the noun it counts: 本 (běn) for bound, page-based items — 一本书 (a book); 张 (zhāng) for flat objects — 一张纸 (a sheet of paper), 一张照片 (a photo); 件 (jiàn) for garments and matters/affairs — 一件衣服 (a piece of clothing), 一件事 (a matter).

条 (tiáo) is for long, narrow, often flexible objects — 一条路 (a road), 一条鱼 (a fish), 一条裤子 (a pair of pants); 双 (shuāng) is specifically for natural pairs — 一双鞋 (a pair of shoes), 一双筷子 (a pair of chopsticks) — used for the pair as a whole, distinct from 两只 for two individual items.

只 (zhī, a different, homophone-only word from the adverb 只 "only") is used for animals and some paired body parts individually — 一只猫 (a cat), 一只手 (a hand); 辆 (liàng) is for wheeled vehicles — 一辆车 (a car), 一辆自行车 (a bicycle).

As with 个, all of these slot into the same Number + Measure Word + Noun structure taught in HSK1 — nothing about the underlying grammar rule changes, only which measure word correctly matches which category of noun. When in doubt, 个 is usually understood even if not perfectly "correct," making it a safe fallback.
pattern: Number + 本/张/件/条/双/只/辆 + N

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū.
Wǒ yǒu yí jiàn hóngsè de yīfu.
Tā mǎi le yí liàng xīn chē.

chapter: Chapter 15: Brief and Tentative Actions — 一下 and Verb Reduplication
title: 一下 and Verb Reduplication (AA / A一A)
theory: 一下 (yíxià), placed directly after a verb, softens the action into something brief, casual, or tentative — "just a bit," "for a moment," roughly like adding "just" or "a sec" in English: 我看一下 (Wǒ kàn yíxià), "Let me take a quick look." It doesn't literally mean the action takes exactly one instance/unit of time — it's a politeness/casualness softener more than a literal quantity.

Verb reduplication — repeating a one-syllable verb twice in a row, either as AA (看看, kànkan) or with 一 inserted, A一A (看一看, kàn yi kàn) — achieves a very similar softening effect to 一下: 你看看 and 你看一下 both mean roughly "take a look," interchangeably in most everyday contexts. Reduplicated forms are typically read with the second syllable in a light, neutral tone.

Two-syllable verbs reduplicate as ABAB, not AABB: 介绍介绍 (jièshào jièshào, "give a bit of an introduction") repeats the whole two-syllable unit, rather than splitting and doubling each syllable separately.

Both 一下 and verb reduplication are especially common in polite requests and suggestions, softening what would otherwise sound like a blunt command: 请等一下 (Qǐng děng yíxià), "Please wait a moment," and 我们商量商量 (Wǒmen shāngliang shāngliang), "Let's discuss it a bit," both feel gentler than their bare-verb equivalents.

examples.english: Let me take a quick look.

chapter: Chapter 16: More Modal Verbs and Prohibition — 别, 应该, 可能, 得 (děi)
title: 别 (bié) — "Don't"
theory: 别 (bié), placed directly before a verb, is the most common everyday way to tell someone not to do something — a direct imperative negation: 别说话 (Bié shuōhuà), "Don't talk." It's functionally very close to HSK1's 不要, and the two are largely interchangeable in commands, though 别 is generally the more frequent, casual, default choice in speech.

别 very often pairs with 了 at the end of the sentence when telling someone to stop an action already in progress, rather than preventing one that hasn't started: 别哭了 (Bié kū le), "Stop crying" (you're already crying) — this trailing 了 is the same change-of-state 了 from HSK1, marking the requested new state (not-crying) as the point of the command.

A softened, more suggestion-like version prefaces the whole phrase with 你 to sound like personal advice rather than a bare command: 你别担心 (Nǐ bié dānxīn), "Don't worry" (advice/reassurance) reads gentler than a bare 别担心 issued to a stranger.

examples.english: Don't forget to bring your wallet.

chapter: Chapter 16: More Modal Verbs and Prohibition — 别, 应该, 可能, 得 (děi)
title: 应该 — Should/Ought To
theory: 应该 (yīnggāi), placed before a verb, expresses obligation or advisability — what one should or ought to do, based on reason, morality, or good sense: 你应该多运动 (Nǐ yīnggāi duō yùndòng), "You should exercise more." It sits in the same modal-verb slot as HSK1's 想/要/会/能.

应该 also extends to expressing a confident expectation about how things probably are, closer to "should be [true]" as a guess rather than an obligation: 他应该到了 (Tā yīnggāi dào le), "He should have arrived by now" (a reasoned expectation, not a command directed at him).

Negation with 不应该 states that something ought NOT to be done: 你不应该这么说 (Nǐ bù yīnggāi zhème shuō), "You shouldn't say that." This differs meaningfully from 别/不要 (a direct command not to do something right now) — 不应该 is a judgment about what's right or wise in general, not necessarily an in-the-moment instruction.

examples.english: He should have arrived by now.

chapter: Chapter 16: More Modal Verbs and Prohibition — 别, 应该, 可能, 得 (děi)
title: 可能 and 得 (děi) — Possibility and Necessity
theory: 可能 (kěnéng) expresses possibility — "maybe/might," a guess with less confidence than 应该's expectation: 他可能不知道 (Tā kěnéng bù zhīdào), "He might not know." 可能 can be used as an adverb before the verb, exactly as shown, or as a standalone comment: 可能吧 (Kěnéng ba), "Maybe."

得 — here read děi, second tone, a completely different reading from the neutral-tone 得 (de) complement particle covered in Chapter 8 (context and tone are the only way to tell them apart in speech) — expresses a strong, often circumstance-driven necessity, "must/have to": 我得走了 (Wǒ děi zǒu le), "I have to go [now]." 得 (děi) tends to feel more urgent/immediate than 应该, and more casual/spoken than the more formal 必须.

得 (děi) is not negated with 不得 — negating necessity instead switches to 不用 (búyòng, "don't need to"), since "don't have to" is a different logical statement (absence of necessity) from "must not" (prohibition, which uses 不能 or 不可以): 你不用来 (Nǐ búyòng lái), "You don't have to come" — not 你不得来.
pattern: S + 可能 + V/Adj。　·　S + 得(děi) + V(+O)。

chapter: Chapter 17: Opinions and Plans — 觉得, 认为, 打算, 准备
title: 觉得 and 认为 — Expressing Opinions
theory: 觉得 (juéde) introduces a personal feeling, impression, or opinion, taking a full clause as its object: 我觉得这个电影很好看 (Wǒ juéde zhège diànyǐng hěn hǎokàn), "I think this movie is good" (literally "I feel [that] this movie is very good-looking"). It's the everyday, casual default for "I think..." in conversation.

认为 (rènwéi) also means "to think/believe," but leans more formal and more reasoned/analytical than 觉得 — closer to "I believe/hold the view that..." — common in more considered statements, debates, or writing: 我认为这个决定是对的 (Wǒ rènwéi zhège juédìng shì duì de), "I believe this decision is correct." In casual daily speech, 觉得 is far more frequent overall.

Both verbs take their opinion as a following clause with no special connecting word needed. Negating the opinion itself (rather than the fact of holding it) happens inside that following clause: 我觉得这个不好 (Wǒ juéde zhège bù hǎo), "I don't think this is good" (not 我不觉得这个好, which is also grammatical but subtly different — "I don't [really] think this is good," doubting the claim itself).

examples.hanzi: 我觉得这个电影很好看。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zhège diànyǐng hěn hǎokàn.
examples.english: I think this movie is good.
I don't think this is good.

examples.hanzi: 我认为这个决定是对的。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ rènwéi zhège juédìng shì duì de.
examples.english: I believe this decision is correct.

chapter: Chapter 17: Opinions and Plans — 觉得, 认为, 打算, 准备
title: 打算 and 准备 — Making Plans
theory: 打算 (dǎsuàn), placed before a verb, means "to plan to," stating an intention that's been thought through, more concrete than the simple desire expressed by HSK1's 想: 我打算明年去中国 (Wǒ dǎsuàn míngnián qù Zhōngguó), "I'm planning to go to China next year." 打算 can also be used as a noun meaning "plan(s)": 你有什么打算？ (Nǐ yǒu shénme dǎsuàn?), "What are your plans?"

准备 (zhǔnbèi), placed before a verb, means "to prepare to / be about to," often carrying a stronger sense of imminent readiness than 打算's more general future intention: 我准备走了 (Wǒ zhǔnbèi zǒu le), "I'm getting ready to go." As a standalone verb, 准备 also simply means "to prepare [something]": 准备晚饭 (zhǔnbèi wǎnfàn), "prepare dinner."

In practice the two overlap heavily in casual speech, but a useful rule of thumb: 打算 sits further out in time and is more about a considered intention, while 准备 sits closer to the present and is more about active readiness — closely related in spirit to Chapter 1's 快要/就要...了, though 准备 itself is the modal verb rather than the aspect marker.

examples.english: I'm planning to go to China next year.

chapter: Chapter 18: Remaining Connectors and Adverbs — 或者, 多/少 + Verb, 一直, 用, 只
title: 或者 — "Or" in Statements
theory: 或者 (huòzhě) means "or," used in plain statements rather than questions — the statement-form counterpart to HSK1's 还是, which is reserved specifically for either/or questions: 你可以喝茶或者咖啡 (Nǐ kěyǐ hē chá huòzhě kāfēi), "You can drink tea or coffee" (a statement offering a choice, not a question).

Using 还是 in a plain statement, or 或者 in a genuine either/or question, is a common and noticeable mistake — the two are not interchangeable despite both meaning "or": 你喝茶还是咖啡？ (question, correct) vs. 你喝茶或者咖啡 (statement, correct).
或者...或者... can also repeat to link more than two options within a statement: 或者你来，或者我去，都可以 (Huòzhě nǐ lái, huòzhě wǒ qù, dōu kěyǐ), "Either you come, or I go — either is fine."

examples.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ hē chá huòzhě kāfēi.
examples.english: You can drink tea or coffee.

examples.hanzi: 我们可以坐公共汽车或者坐地铁。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen kěyǐ zuò gōnggòng qìchē huòzhě zuò dìtiě.
examples.english: We can take the bus or the subway.

examples.hanzi: 或者你来，或者我去，都可以。
examples.pinyin: Huòzhě nǐ lái, huòzhě wǒ qù, dōu kěyǐ.
examples.english: Either you come, or I go — either is fine.

examples.hanzi: 你可以写信或者打电话告诉我。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ xiě xìn huòzhě dǎ diànhuà gàosu wǒ.
examples.english: You can write a letter or call to tell me.

chapter: Chapter 18: Remaining Connectors and Adverbs — 或者, 多/少 + Verb, 一直, 用, 只
title: 多/少 + Verb — Doing More/Less of Something
theory: 多 (duō, "more") and 少 (shǎo, "less") can sit directly before a verb, telling someone to do more or less of that action: 多喝水 (duō hē shuǐ), "drink more water"; 少吃糖 (shǎo chī táng), "eat less sugar." This is distinct from 多 as a question word for measurements (HSK1, 多高/多长) — here it's a plain adverbial quantity-adjective, not part of a question.

This pattern is extremely common in advice and gentle commands: 多穿点儿衣服 (duō chuān diǎnr yīfu), "put on more clothes"; 多休息 (duō xiūxi), "get more rest." 一点儿 (HSK1) often tags along after the object for a softer, more casual feel.

Negating this pattern is unusual — instead of 不多喝水, the natural way to discourage an action uses 别 or 不要 elsewhere. 少 + Verb already inherently means "do less of X," making 多/少 a matched positive/negative pair rather than one needing separate negation.

examples.pinyin: Tiān lěng le, duō chuān diǎnr yīfu.
examples.english: It's cold, put on more clothes.

chapter: Chapter 18: Remaining Connectors and Adverbs — 或者, 多/少 + Verb, 一直, 用, 只
title: 一直 — Continuously/All Along
theory: 一直 (yìzhí), placed before a verb, describes an action or state as continuing without interruption, either "continuously" over a stretch of time or "all along/the whole time" from a given starting point: 我一直在等你 (Wǒ yìzhí zài děng nǐ), "I've been waiting for you the whole time" (often paired naturally with the progressive 在/正在, since continuous waiting is itself an ongoing action).

一直 also works for describing an unchanging state or habitual fact stretching back over time: 他一直很忙 (Tā yìzhí hěn máng), "He's always/consistently been busy," 我一直不知道这件事 (Wǒ yìzhí bù zhīdào zhè jiàn shì), "I never knew about this."

一直 differs from 还 in emphasis: 还 focuses on the fact that a state persists as of NOW, right up to the present moment ("still"), while 一直 emphasizes the unbroken continuity of the whole stretch of time — the two often overlap in a single sentence, and can even combine: 他一直还没回来 (Tā yìzhí hái méi huílái), "He still hasn't come back this whole time."

examples.english: I've been waiting for you the whole time.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yìzhí bù zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.

examples.english: He still hasn't come back this whole time.

chapter: Chapter 18: Remaining Connectors and Adverbs — 或者, 多/少 + Verb, 一直, 用, 只
title: 用 (yòng) — Means and Instruments
theory: 用 (yòng) as a coverb, placed before a verb, marks the tool, method, or means used to carry out an action, "using/with": 用筷子吃饭 (yòng kuàizi chīfàn), "eat with chopsticks"; 用中文说 (yòng Zhōngwén shuō), "say [it] in Chinese." Like every coverb phrase covered so far (给/对, 从...到...), the 用-phrase goes before the main verb it modifies.

用 also functions as an ordinary standalone verb meaning simply "to use": 我可以用一下你的手机吗？ (Wǒ kěyǐ yòng yíxià nǐ de shǒujī ma?, using 一下 from Chapter 15 to soften the request), "Can I use your phone for a moment?" — here 用 is the main verb of the sentence, not a coverb introducing another verb.

A common everyday pattern combines 用 with a language name to specify what language something is done in — 用英语怎么说？ (Yòng Yīngyǔ zěnme shuō?), "How do you say it in English?" — reusing 怎么 from HSK1's question-word chapter.

examples.hanzi: 我可以用一下你的手机吗？
examples.pinyin: Wǒ kěyǐ yòng yíxià nǐ de shǒujī ma?
examples.english: Can I use your phone for a moment?

examples.pinyin: Zhège zì yòng Yīngyǔ zěnme shuō?
examples.english: How do you say this word in English?

chapter: Chapter 18: Remaining Connectors and Adverbs — 或者, 多/少 + Verb, 一直, 用, 只
title: 只 (zhǐ) — Only
theory: 只 (zhǐ), placed before a verb or a quantity, restricts a statement to exactly the item(s) mentioned and nothing more, "only": 我只有一个哥哥 (Wǒ zhǐ yǒu yí ge gēge), "I only have one older brother." It sits in the same adverb-before-verb slot as 也/都/一起/还/一直.
只 very often pairs with 有 (as above) or directly before a number/quantity to sharply limit it: 只要五分钟 (zhǐ yào wǔ fēnzhōng), "it only takes/needs five minutes" — reusing 要 in its "need/require" sense.

只是 (zhǐshì) — 只 plus 是 — forms a related but distinct fixed phrase meaning "merely/it's just that," often used to downplay or clarify a point rather than strictly counting a quantity: 我只是想问一下 (Wǒ zhǐshì xiǎng wèn yíxià), "I just wanted to ask [something, no big deal]."

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zhǐ yǒu yí ge gēge.
examples.english: I only have one older brother.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì zhǐ yào wǔ fēnzhōng.
Tā zhǐ huì shuō yìdiǎnr Yīngyǔ.
examples.english: He can only speak a little English.
